NOTHING Mean About Him—The extremist. A WOMAN is sometimes minded better when she isn't strong minded. No one can define love, although we all know it by heart. A man never realises his worth until he is sued for breach of promise. WHEN a woman's face is her fortune, old age sends her into bankruptcy. "THERE is no place like home," provided it isn't one where you are labelled an "inmate." Favours is one of those things which you can best keep in by asking for none of it. LEISURE is the condition in which you have to work hard without pay in order to kill the time. A COUNTRY village is the best place for the young fellow who wants to be a "prominent mer- chant." "NEARLY all these Arctic explorers seem to make one or two fatal mistakes." "Yes "They either starve or freeze to death." AN EMBARRASSMENT OF RICHF.S.—Not knowing Whether the girl loves yen, or your money. OF all birds, the tailor's goose has the most prominent bill. WHEN a man gets a hearing in court, he is likely to heae something that he doesn't like. Ox: "Why did you pursue that red dress so precipitately?' Bull "it struck me that there weren't gores enough in it". QUANTITY AND QUALITY.—A marquis said to a banker, "I would have you to know, sir, that lens a man of quality." "And I," replied the banker, " a man of quantity, my lord. WHEN a sportsman tires into a covey of par- tridges, he makes them all quail. PHILOSOPIIICAL.—" I never have any kind of lucs," said Mawson. " I hatai luck enough," slid Dawson, who had been having nothing bat bad luck." A FASHIONABLE lady's-maid. who endeavours to rival her mistr- as in the style of her garments, wrote an order to the perfumer the other day and requested him to forward a case of "0 Dick Alone!" RIGHTEOUS RESENTMENT. Mrs. O'Toole: "What did yez say to Missus Reagan whin she insulted yes ? " Mrs. Rader ty : "Faith, I didn't -say nothin'. I jist done it !' -THE ONLY REASON.—TOM: "I proposed fast enough, but she wouldn't have me." Jack: "Did she give you any reason?" Tom: "No; except that she didn't care forme." FIG: "It's curious a half-moon is heavier than a full one." Fog: "How is that?" Fig: "The full moon is the lightest, isn't it?" " \Vitali are pauses?" asked the teacher of her aims of small boys. "Things that grow on catses," answered Tommy Tomlins. WHAT nonsense it is to say that a man is "inclined to be bald!" When a man is becoming bald, it is generally quite against his inclination. SPIFKINS : "Are you aware tat the United States census embraces sixteen million women ? " Softbrain "Hai Jove! who would not be a Census ! " DIFFERENCES.—Wog : "You're a different man since you've been married, Spooker." Spooker " Yes ? I only wish my wife were a ditlerent woman!" CORNERED.—CharIie Isbroke : "I cannot pay you to-day. You see, my bootmaker has just been here and"— Tailor: "Yes, I met, him on the way up, and he said you put him off Lecause you'd got to pay your tailor to-day. So here's the bill, air." MADAM," said old Roger to his boarding house keeper, "in primitive countries beef is often legal tender ; but, madam," said he, emphatically thrust- ing his fork into the steak," "all the law in 'Christendom could not make this beef tender !" "1 wisu you would not smoke cigars," said a plump little black-eyed girl to her lover. "Why may I nst as well smoke as your chimney!" "Because chimneys don't smoke when they are in good order." He has given up smoking. "Who was the first man?" asked a Chicago teacher of his class. "Washington," promptly answered the head boy. " You are wrong,' said the teacher: "Adam was the first man.' "Oh, well, I daresay you are right,' said the young patriot, " if you refer to furriners." A YOUNG apprentice to the shoemaking business asked his master what answer he should give to the often-repeated question. " Does your master warrant his shoes? ' "Answer, Thomas," said the master, "That I warrant them to prove good, and if they don't I'll make them good for nothing." No IMPROVEMENT.—Father (after thrashing his little son) : " When I was a bad boy my father always used to thrash me." Little Son (sulkily): "It doesn't seem to have made you any better ' CUSTOMER: "I'm looking for a tall man with one arm." Floorwalker: " Certo i ily. The remnant counter is just across the store." Jacx : "I called on Miss Fiiz last night, but didn't stay long, as she was complaining that her teeth ached." Jei-s : "Isn't it a shame! And it was such en ex °naive set, too !" TEACHER "Yes, Willie; every day will be Sunday in heaven." Willie: "Well, what day will they hold tiieir Sunday school picnics on?" " WHAT lovely bachelor apartments Browser has ! But they say he has strange doings there." ," ?es ; I fancy hie room is better than his company." SEA-SICK PASSENGER: "Captain, are you sure the boat is staunch eavugh to weather this gale?" Captain: "Made of seasoned oak, sir.' Sea-sick Passenger: "Glad to hear it. Thought by the way it was plunging it was Made of piterapine !" VERY SIMPLE.—A merchant examining a hogs- head of hardware, on comparing it with the invoice, found it all right, except a hammer short. "Och, don't be troubled," said the Irish porter: "sure the nagur took it out to open the hogshead with 1" DEFICIENT IN SPELLING.—" Don't you think that if your education had been what it should have been, you would have kept out of gaol ?" said a visitor to a prisoner. "I reckon so. I wrote another man's name on a cheque, and got caught because I hadn't spelled it right." BEYOND HOPE.—" This," said the attendant, as he led the way through the incurable ward, "is one of the worst cases we have. He was once a 'newspaper man." "But what is his hallucina- tion?" asked the visitor, anxiously. "He thinks he has money," answered the attendant, sadly. A FEW years since, at the celebration of a national anniversary, a poor pedlar who was pre- sent, being asked for a toast, gave the following : "Here's a health to poverty ; it sticks to a man when all his friends have deserted him." OFFICER (to new cavalry recruit) : "Never approach the horses from behind without speaking. If you do, they'll kick you in that thick head of yours, and the end of it will be we shall have nothing but lame horses in the squadron !" FATHER: "Doctor, I have come to see you about my little boy." Doctor: " What is the matter with him?" Father: "One leg is shorter than 'the other, and he limps. Now, what would you do in such a case?" Doctor: "I think I should limp, too." A YOUNG man, visiting his sweetheart, met a rival who was somewhat advanced in years, and wishing to rally him, inquired how old he was. " I can't exactly tell," replied the other ; "but I can inform you that an ass is older at twenty than a man at sixty !" , A COMMON MISTAKE.—" You flatter me, madam," said a fop upon being told by a lady that nis hat was a very fine one. "Not at all, sir replied she ; " I only praise the hatter ; had the head or face been worth notice, I should not have thought of the hat." A HINT TO ADVERTISERS.—A bookseller adver- tises " !Ikew Children's Books." This is somewhat like the man who advertised " Red Children's Stockings—Black Men's Leather Gloves—Plain Ladies' Fur Soles—and Mahogany Children's Chairs !" WOULDN'T BE DICTATED To.—Wool: "1 sawa post-card the other day dropped in the office by a woman ; the front was written full, with only the address on the back." Van Pelt: "There is a line on the front of the card which forbids that." Wool: "That was the only way I could account for it." STAGE MANAGER (of the Farce Comedy COM- pany): "What'll we do? The men have made a *"1"--- mistake and set the stage for the third act instead of the first! ' Proprietor : " That's all right. Tell 'em to go ahead with the third act, and have the first afterwards. Nobody will know the difference!" -

LADIES' LETTER. —..)rd Kelvin, the President of the Royal Society, who is one of the figure-heads at most of the great my Dzmaar N dinners of the season, is one of our most succes/ful Patentees. Among the most important of :'his Blue flowers are very popular for wearing with patents, both from the view of money and fame, is our hats, and cornflowers especially are the rage. that which corrects the magnetic variations of the These are usually found in company with a blue compass both as regards the " true pole' and the dress. They look very well on black hats, which sffect of the iron used in building ships—a patent are being very much worn. A very popular style adopted in our own and other navies and in many of hat is of coarse bright green straw, wide of our great merchant ships. brimmed, and high crowned, and trimmed with . huge bows of shot green and blue ribbon, blue cornflowers, and tall spikes of green grass, or in some cases the flowers shade from deep purple to palest blue, and the shot ribbon has a plain purple edge; but such eccentricities are scarcely suitable for those who cannot afford more than a couple of summer hats, which have to be worn, perhaps, with five or sit gowns. A rough green straw sailor, too, although not such a useful "all round" hat, is pretty; trimmed will a ruche of chiffon, 'erect tufts of lilies of the valley and their leaves at the sides, while a stylish model has a wide brim of black fancy straw, picturesquely crumpled up here and there, and a transparent crown of cream lace, the trimming consisting of bows of pink and green chin 6 ribbon and pale pink poppies, arranged as a half wreath, with a few' nestled under the brim at the left side towards the front. Veils of cream or white lace are much worn, and with wide-brimmed hats double-width nets are almost invariably used, in spite of the 'dis- comfort caused in hot weather by the folds beneath the chin. As regards toques they are being worn as much as ever. One sees many pretty oncsworn. An immensely charming one I saw at a garden party the other day was made in gold-coloured lace and pearls of the same shade, with bows at each side of turquoise gauze ribbon, striped with satin. There was a black aigrette at one side. Neck mufflers are worn with toques more than with hats.

The Earl of Dysart, who has renounced the Gov- I ernment and all its work, has been a singularly 1 unstable politician. As a young man he professed himself a Liberal, and there was much growling ! when Mr. Gladstone appointed him Lord Lieutenant, of Rutland in 1881 because he was but twenty-two years of age, and ownod about as many acres in that tiny shire. In 1886 he joined himself to the Dissentients, and actively supported the Unionist candidate for Grantham, but just before the General Election of 1892 he temporarily saw the error of tis ways, and came in line with his old friends. This, therefore, is his third face-about in ten years,so that his defection may fairly be regarded as nigligeable by the Liberals. _

At the military clubs there is the greatest sym- pathy with Mr. Campbell-Banneiman. Liberal War Ministers are not always favourites with mili- tary officers, but Mr. Campbell-Bannerman is cer- tainly the most popular War Minister of the gsner- ation. It is not only that he has shown a real desire TO improve the position of the officer and the soldier, but that he has revealed a practical and businesc-like celerity in re-arming the army which lies surprised military men accustomed to other official methods.

Di-msing the pout as to who will be the new I Commander-in-ChieLa well-informed correspondent I writes that the Duke of Connaught's chance of suc- ceeding to the post is a very poor one unless the Tories come hack in very great numbers at the General Election. Some of the Liberal Unionists declare that they will not countenance the appoint- ment of another Royal Duke, and a job of this sort would certainly lead to an immense outcry from a Liberal Opposition. It is more likely that the Duke of Connaught will get the appointment now held by Lord Roberts when the general re-arrange- ment takes place.

The Ehahzada was evidently more pleased with the Royal Show at Darlington than with most of the great functicns in which he has taken a part ,ince he has been in England. He watched with interest the operation of shearing sheep by machi- nery, and of milking cows with a steam engine. Rig criticism on English breeds of lire stock was that they were all too fat—a criticism which is not without some foundation at a show like the I Royal, which is not a Christmas Fat Stock Show

Mr. Gladstone's fellow-voyagers have brought home a budget of pleasant stories about Sir Donald t:urrie's chief guest. When the general invitation was given to the Danes to visit the Tantalion Castle, there was an immediate rush to see " the great Gladstone." There he sat in the shade, with a hook which deeply engrossed his attention, and sit the time when successive scores were discussing him and gazing at him, Mr. Gladstone went on reading. A little cord was placed at a short di,- twice from his chair to ward off too clo-e a visit iron; his numerous admirers. One who witnessed the arrival of the King and Queen of Denmark says that the meeting between the monarch Imo the statesman was quite touching in its friendliness. The King was moved to tears by the kindly elo- quence of Mr. Gladstone in his allusions to the Princess of Wales, and the Queen was also deeply affected. Mrs. Gladstone's constant care over her husband was very interesting to witness. She was especially anxious to protect Mr. Gladstone from cold, and it was amusing to notice how impetu- ously be threw off the rug which she had with forethought placed over his knees when sitting on deck. It has been somewhat of a reproach to F.nglisb watering-places that they lack the brighter enter- tainments of Continental resorts. Eastbourne is striving hard to dispel this idea. There is to he n battle of flowers ond also a rose fete there on July 26 and 27. Prizes amounting to 2.100 in value are ffered for coaches, carriages, and riding horses. presumably florally adorned, and the than hall is to be the scene of " red and white rose ball." These colours have a distinct historical flavour.

I was speaking just now of blue dresses, which are very much de rigeur in Paris just now, in fact, I am told that a blue crepon dress is one of the necessities of the Frenchwoman's ' existence. A • curious note is often stuck on these blue gowns by a vivid emerald- green sash. Curious though this may be, it is un- doubtedly attractive. The green must be Pure emerald, and have but little yellow in its depths. Besides this combination of emerald green and blue, let me recommend heliotrope and blue. A seasonable dress has a skirt in marron crepon, very full, anti the bodice is of pink crepe de Chine. There are large sleeves, with deep gauntlets of the marron, covered N ith cream appliqué lace, and a large collarette of pink chine ribbon, frill of cream lace. Tht . chemisette and collar are of lace over marron. There is a folded ribbon band, with Japanese bow. The hat is in coarse shaded straw, with lace to match that on the costume, and has large full pink bows and bunches of green rose leaves.

Blouses, as you know, are being worn in all colours. Most of them have accordeon-pleated sleeves to the elbows. and collars of lace or. batiste at the back, ending in pointed pieces in the front. These deep collars are very picturesque, but they do not suit everybody, being rather trying to all but the best complexions. I saw a square one the other morning made of cream-coloured satin, and trimmed with a double ruffle of deep yellow lace, split up the back the same as it was in front. It made its brunette wearer look perfectly lovely, the cream colour and deep yellow neutralising the sallow of her skin and bringing out all its creaminess and pinkness to perfection. But then a moment later we saw a white collar on a pale anwmic looking girl, who looked simply ghastly from the proximity of this trying mass of dead white. ABother fashion- able blouse is in glace silk, with a large green and pink plaid. The balloon sleeves have deep gaunt- lets of white muslin drawn over pink silk straps. Collar and double epaulettes are of white muslin with earn guipure.

For little girls nothing is more suitable and pretty for wear in the country and at the seaside than serge sailor frocks, and the best material is Egerton Burnett's unrivalled serge, which is impervious alike to salt and fresh water. The frock should be of navy serge, and I should advise materfamilias to have it made with several blouses, one of navy serge to match the skirt, trimmed with narrow black purl braid, and the others of white or pale blue washing drill, trimmed with white purl braid. The sleeves button at the wristband. The vest, in any case, should be of warm white serge or flannel, as even in the hottest weather, children are most liable to oontract colds on the chest.
Vour loving JENNIE.

Sir John Thorold, the retiring President of the R.A.S.E., bears one of the oldest names in rngland. His family dates back in a direct line to Saxon times. Tumid was on of Harold's ArrihnssFdors to Wil:iatn, and hi portrait may be seen on the Boyorix Tapestry. Sir John's successor cannot boast of such long decent, but no man had done more for agri- culture than Sir ‘Valter Gilhey. The herd of dairy cattle and the stud of hackneys and shires at P.lsen- ham are known all over the world. and Sir Walter is indefatigable in his eft qts in this direction.

The gentleman ...vho now occupies the proud position of the wrocksr of the Government, the Hon. St. John Brodrick. M.P.. is the eldest son of Viscount Middleton. fie is thirty-six years of age, but looks considerably older. So grave is his demeanour that even at Oxford he was sometimes called "Ptin.e Minister Brodrick," and his austerity in presiding over the Union of the Univ..l.sity was the general theme of comment. He was returned for , West Surrey in 1880, immediately after leaving the ' University. Mr. Brodrick was Financial Score' cry to the War Office, and is rsgtirded cs one of the promiAng young men of the Tory Party. His wife is a daughter of Lord Wemvss.

Golf apparently is the only specific for Mr. Bal- four when his nerves are shrieked or lowered. and to polf he nsorted after the Tory victory with grim and silent determination. But at night he looked as worried as ever. He was seen riding in aI brougham with one of his political friends. . abstractedly fanning himself with his hat, and : doubtless thinking that it was now in the pow f r of his political opponents to put him into a remark- ably tight corner if they wished. Another corres- pondent says that Mr. Balfmr looked like n. man who had received a sudden and unexpecte I !low, rather than a politician who had gained his heart's desire, and the correspondent says he has it on ' good authority that when he met a few of his colleagu.s in private conference a short time after the division he was half dazed and altogtther ir,ropte. 1. The lirgering hope that Mr. Gladstone would throw himself into the criming battle is at an end, , and with the dissolution of Parliament he will retire from public life. It is strange to read of him. in the thick of a great Ministerial crisis, as a quiet student of Bishop Butler in the British Museum. The most that is now to be expected from him is a farewell manifesto to his prestaconstituents,which at the same time will be through them a manifesto to the Liberal party. Some sanguine • Radicals ardently believed that he would once more put himself at the head of the party, and take his place again as the chief figure in the house of :Commons. This was tarftamount to laying upon ' him the task of once more undergoing the fearfill ordeal OF introducing and passing a Home Rule Bill, if he succeeded in. bringing his party back into office. Mr. Gladstone's constitution is not now equal I to a task of such enormous magnitude and labosr. If be had been seduced by the tempter to leave the serenity of his studies in literature and theology. and come back to office and power, the Bill to the passing of which he would have bent his whole energies would have been a Home Rule Bill. All the other great measures of the present session would have stood in abeyance, and at the end of his own session he would have had his Bill rejected by the Lords, and would in another flaming oration have placed the Liberal party in the position to which he had led it at his retirement—of standing face to I face with the obstructiv- Chamber, and with the I different line of policy in front of it. Such hns been the hope of many Radicals in the present crieis,ancl they have heard with sorrow that the aged states- man leaves the lead to other hands.

The idea is gaining ground that the composition of the new Ministry is intended to be only t.moo- rary. Lord Salisbury's acceptance of the Foreign Secretaryship has been, as I anticipated. received with much disfavour by his supporters generally. The universal impression is that he must neglect the duties of the Prime Minister in order to attend to those of the Foreign Secretary. Still lees popu- lar is the alleged appointment of Lord Belgium, to the Lord Chancellorship. It is well known (her a section of the old-fashioned Tories made a dead set in his behalf, and that Lord Salisbury has from the first been a stnng partisan of Lord Halstrurv, to whom he has been in the habit of looking for advice and assistance. But certain appointments which ' his Lordship made when he was last in office are not forgotten even on his own side of politics. and, to put it mildly, his is certainly not a popular appointment.

Guonod's mother was fond of painting and music. Iceland has fewer cases of phthisis than any ther country on the globe. Of every 100 eases of cataract, ffty-four are males and forty-six females. The organised charities of Great Britain give away every year over £10,000,000. Mr. Gladstone once said, "I hate getting up in the morning, and hate it the same every morning." 1 The Prince of Wales has said that his sister, the Empress Frederick, is the cleverest woman he has ever met. In France it is a punishable offence for anyone to give infants under one year any form of solid food unless such be ordered by written prescription signed by a legally qualified medical man. Vineg ir and yeast should never las kept in stone jars for there is an acid in them vel:c.h attacks the glazing, and mixing with it has a poisoning property. There are some vegetables that can scarcely be dis- tinguished from animals, and some animals that seem to have all the characteristics of vegetables. There are no undertakers in Japan. When a person dies it is the custom for his nearest relatives to put him into a cwffin and bury him, and the mourning does not begin until after burial. Among the many unforeseen results of the war be- tween China and Japan is an enormous diminution in the supply of camphor, and unless some serviceable sub- stitute can be found, the maths are likely to hold high carnival among our put away clothes are long. Although she is famous fur her charity, and for the keen interest that she takes in the welfare of her sub- jects, the Queen of Italy is greatly given to display in dress, and is certainly the most extravagant woman in her husband's kingdom. The King, indeed, often re- proves her for the example which she sets her subjects, although, be it said, the women of Italy need little en- couragement in the matter of dress. The Queen's love of display, and especially of wearing jewels, amounts to a passion, and she would rather economise in any other way than by curtailing her jewellers' or her dress- makers' bill. The fair sex will says " Science Siftings." do well to be wary of the " Answers to Correspondents" of a medical nature that adorn the columns of some of our contemporaries. These should not be taken too seriously. The editor of a well-known ladies' paper told a convivial company of " New Vagabonds "how one week. casually overlooking the " Answers to Correspondents " column, which was entrusted to a lady journalist, he read the following alarming statement,together with the business like addendum :—" Martha.—The reply given last week was a mistake. You should have used ± gr. of strych- nine, not ± lb. Jay's is the best house for mourning."
Oil for the Face.

If you have been out all day, or come from a journey, or if you have had a hard day's work and you want to get thoroughly clean, don't wash your face with soap and water. Grease or oil is far better, as it enters and cleanses the pores of the skin. Learn a le*ion from the actresses. If an actress were to wash with soap and 1 water the nightly make-up from her face she would. have no skin to speak of in a week, to say nothing of a complexion. Apply a little grease or oil, and after a few minutes rub thoroughly, first with a soft towel, and then with a piece of chamois leather. To demonstrate that this cleans the Sail] more thoroughly, some day,after a journey, just wash your lee with soap and water as well as you can; then cover it with grease or oil and remove with a soft cloth. One glance at the cloth will show that soap and water did not get it clean.

Drinks for Workers in Warm Weather. STOKOS—Put from four to six ounces of fresh oatmeal," ground as fine as flour, into a pan, mix with a little cold 1 water to the substance of cream, then add five or six ' ounces of loaf sugar, and a fresh lemon cut in thin slices, with the pips taken out. Add a gallon of boiling. water. Stir thoroughly while the water is being poured on. Drink hot,warm,or cold. The lemon may be omitted, or any other flavouring used instead. The cost is 3d. gallon,or five gallons for is.; four lemons are enough for five gallons. EIoPICOS..-80i1 of hops and I z of ginger (bruised) in 1 gallons of water for 25 minutes ; add Ilb. of best brown sugar and boil ten minutes more, then strain land bottle or put into a cask while hot • it will he ready for drinking when cold. It should b.; kept in a cool place. No yeast must be used. Dried horehound may be substituted for hims. Cost 3d. a gallon. , 1 LEMONADI. for pent use .—Put Ilb. of white sugar, lrz cream of tartar, and two lemons cut in slices, in a largo jug, and pour over all 3 quarts of boiling water. A teaspoonful of essence of lemon may be used instead of lemons This is a very cooling drink, and costs about 2d. a quart. For hottling.—Disenlve 21bs. of lump sugar in a quart of boiling water,aini 2n. of citric acid, and 2 lemons sliced (or a teaspoor ful of es,etice of lemon) ; stir toge- ther, strain, and bottle when cold. A teaspoonful in a glasa ef water will make a pleasant drink. Costs about Is 3d. a quart, which will make 5 or 6 quarts of drink. Note.—One ',mon is about squat 10 10 drops of essence of lemon, or to drachm of citric acid. If essence of lemon is used in place of the lemon it should be mixed in when it is lukewarm.

div.head: MONK'S CATTLE
div.p: MONK'S CATTLE

At Chißingham, as is well-known, there exists a hord I of pure bred native wild cattle, and scattered up and down the country are other isolated examples of old historic breeds. At a recent Sale at Bury St. Edmmul's a famous herd of pure descendants of the old "Monk's cattle " was put up to auction. These animals have come down unmixed from the oldest historic breed of cattle in the British Isles, and have always been re- garded with interest by naturalists. They were ori- ginally selected by the monks, who in their way were the leaders of agriculttire, as being more easily domesti- cated and less adapted to purposes of sport than hormal cattle. At the dissolution of the monastries they were dispersed over the country, and mostly became merzed in the common local breeds. The animals aro polled white, with black or Ted points On the ears, muzzle rltns of eyes and hoofs; and are quaint looking creatures re- side our better known cattle. A large part of the herd was purchased be Mr. A;shetoc-Smith, of Carnarvon- shirerwho has already, at, Vaynol Park, in that count y, an equally unique herd of pure native white-horned cattle with black ears and black muzzles. There are very few really pure breeds of cattle now to be found in England, and none at all among our common domestic herds. In Ireland the Kerry cattle are kept pure un- mixed, and the same is the C3BO with the Jersey and Alderney herds. In the last:named islands so j,,abats are they of the purity of their cattle that they will on no pret,nce allow any living cow or bullock to be landed on their shores, and when any of their waive animals are taken from the islands for exhibition, they will not p r mit them to return alive. At Guernsey, the laws in this respect are more lax, and as a consequence the cattle to be seen on that island is of a more hybrid character than is to be found in tither Jersey or Alderney.

CHAPTER XXXVI. —(Continued). THE next afternoon the Lancasters, accompanied by Karl, presented themselves at Thornton Villa. Doris flew to the door to welcome them, her face all smiles and blushes. They corald scarcely recog• nise in the gay, happy girl who conducted thein into the drawing-room the dreamy eyed, peinAve Doris who had always shrunk in such ahhorrenee from lovers, and the subject of love. When Trixy heard that Karl Lancaster was coming that afternoon, anyone might have guesett her secret, she blushed so hotly to the very roots of her bronze curly head. Doris noticed it at once. She noticed, too how very partieular Beatrix was over her dress that afternoon. - Even Karl Lancaster was bewildered hy the love;y vislon of girlish loveliness that, (hawed into the draWillg room to greet him that extending the prettiest mite of a little white slim
hand. - " Why, I declare. Trixy ! bow you do change " cried Karl, fl:ishing• a little under the five ot the
giri'shlg, spariiliog eye-. " in wnat way ?" asked Trixy, with a toss of her

curls. " You see more: m beautiful each time I see you, ' he deeiaied, honestly. "Indeed, you do, Trixy." He expected some kind of a saucy reply or witty remark, but Trixy answered never a ; pcume from hi iii was be to her. 1.-carl was startled at the swift change that came over the

girl's lovely face. "I hope you are not angry with me for saying that, Trixy,' he added, earnestly. " I inea.ntlo) flattery, upon my honour. We are such old friends, you kit ,w, that I may surely be par- doned for saying just what I think, and know to be true." Trixy laughed, but somehow the laugi:ter seemed slightly forced. " Your mother promised me that you would show me the new clove carnations in the garden. Shall we go and look at them now?" he asked, eager to change the subject, an Trixy agreed at once. How pretty Trixy look as she moved among the glowing roses, Karl told himself. Strange that he had never known how pretty she was before. "I am glad you are here, Karl, that I may say in person that which I was just about to write to you to-day," said Trixy, looking up at him suddenly. "What is that ? " he asked, drawing nearer to her. "I should like you to be best man' at Doris's and Gwendolin's wedding,' sh 3 said. "I am to be first bridesmaid, and am to choose the best man. I should like it to be you Karl, if you are willing." "Do you think me more eligible than any other of your numerous acquaintances that you would confer such an honour upon me :" he asked, lightly, banteringly. "Yes," she answered, seriously. And again he saw that strange look cross her face, and her eyes fell before his searching gaze. A strange sensation thrilled his heart. A sud- den thought flashed through his brain. Trixy cared for him I Surely, it could not be egotistical fancy. The thought brought with it great plea.

They had taken passage on the Servia for Europe, and among the first names of the passengers booked they read Vivian's name. There was an angry exclamation of annoyance on Frederick's face as he came back to their state room and told Doris this. Two white arms stole round his neck, and a lovely, dimpled cheek was pressed close to his. "Do not feel hard against Vivian, Frederick, dear," she said smiling. "Heaven made her our good angel from the very first. If you had not imagined yourself in love with Vivian, and come up to Madame Delmar's seminary, that eventful day, to see about taking her to that ball, I should never have met you, dear." " Why, I declare, that's so !" he said. "I never thought cf that, I'm sure." "And if it had not been for Vivian's coming to Newport, and discovering my identity, I should never have been so desperate as to write th-kt letter to you revealing the truth that I was Doris, whom you mourned as dead." "By George !—pray pardon the expression—but that s true, too, Doris. After all, we do owe a great deal to Vivian." Great was Vivian's consternation to find that Frederick and his bride were on the same steamer • with her, but with the natural polish sociAy gives to the woman of the world she smothered her chagrin, and stepped forward, greeting Doris gracefully. She had been a little fearful lest Doris might have give her the cut direct, but she risked it, and was more than suprised at Doris's sweet, cordial manner toward her. "You took me at my word that night at New- port, Doris," she said. "I do declare to you I never meant one half I said." "Do not let that trouble you, Vivian," answered Doris, with a graetful smile. "It proved the blessing of my life. It re-united me with—my husband." Vivian murmured and smiled and turned away, for she saw Frederick approaching, and she could not bear to witness the little tendernesses that would pass between Doris and her adoring hus- band. "My plotting and planning to keep them apart from first to last has all been in vain," she muttered. "Heaven's will was stronger than the will of woman. It seems they were intended for each other."

sure. He was young and impulsive, and, as his father had said, his heart was on the rebound. He took a step nearer Trixy, and on the impulse of the moment whispered softly, as he caught her little white hand; "Don't you think I could fill a better position at that wedding than a best man,' Trixy? "Why there is no better position, unless you were one of the two bridegrooms," she declared. " Why couldn't there be three bridegro.ms ? " he asked, coolly. "I'm sure I don't know," stammered Trixy, wishing meanwhile that she were back in the drawing-room with the rest of the family. "I think I could fill the position of bridegroom much better, making it a triple wedding, if I could but find a bride," he persisted. "Do you think I could find one, Trixy?" "Perhaps you might find some girl foolish enough to have you," she replied, blushing furi- ously as she turned away from the audacious young fellow, and attempted to fly past him over the lawn • but he held her hands fast. " Would you be willing to try the experiment, Trixy ?" he replied; "it might not be so very foolish." Half an hour afterward, when the lovers re- entered the drawing-room, Doris knew by the happy light on their faces that Karl had found consolation at last. She crossed over to Frederick's side and laid her hand on his arm. "Do you see how happy Trixy is?" she mur- mured. "I am afraid we are soon to lose her, Fm ederick." "if by losing her I shall gain so noble a young moan its Karl for a brother-in-law, I would be quite content. There was a time when I felt quite bitter towards him, Doris, and that was in those old days when I looked upon him as my rival in love's war- fare. He was madly in love with my Doris then, and I half tear is 20 stilL I hope he may not wish to marry poor Trixy through pique," he added, anxiously. "Oh, Frederick, you must not think that," cried ! Doris. "Karl is too nobie for that. I—l—refused his love twice," she whispered, drooping her sweet blushing face; "and the last time, knowing his love was all in vain, he promised me that he would try his best to forget me. Nothing but a deep, reverential, brotherly love remains in his heart for me now." "I am very glad to think that,' said Frederick, so heartily that Doris could not help but laugh. "Are congratulations in order ? " whispered Doris 7 to Karl, as she bade him good-night. "Yes," he answered; ".1 know you will wish me • all her piuess, Doris. I have won for my promised bride the dearest and sweetest girl in the whole wide world, present company excepted," he added. gallantly. ! "I am glad for your sake, Karl," smiled Doris. "Is it to be a triple wedding ?'' " If you are ad agreed," he replied. "Of course, we will all be agreed upon that question," said Doris, heartily; you know that, Karl." Mrs. Lancaster could find no fault with her son's choice. True, the one desire of her heart was that be should marry Doris, but seetng that was out of the question, she was quite willing to receive dark- eyed Beatrix as a daughter. The marriages were set for a month from that " day, Frederick declaring that he would not wait twenty-four hours longer, and that he had waited too long already to claim lovely Doris. Gwendolia's and Trixy's lovers were equally anxious that the marriages should take place as soon as possible. The long-looked-for day arrived at last, and a sunnier, brighter day could never have been wished for.
CitArrEa XXXVIL WEDDING JOY BELLS

PREPARATIONS for the weddings had been going on at Thornton Villa on a grand scale for over a fortnight past, and on. th s eventful morning the house and the grounds presented a veritable fairy- land aptearance. The grounds were a bewildi'ring mass of glow- ing roses ; the fountains, with their tinted waters, . sparkled like rainbows in the sun; wherever the eye turned it was greeted by banks of thdicate blooms. Long ere the sun had set the gusts began to arrive, and a gayer, merrier throng never made the grim old walls of Thornton Villa echo with their laughter. One by one the marriages were solemnised. First, Gwendolin and Gerald Mar- ston's, then Beatrix and Karl's, then, last of all, Doris and Frederick took their places beneath the great horse shoe of white Lilies, and the words were spoken which gave Frederick, fur the second time, sweet Doris for his bride. The congratulations and the grand wedding breakfast were over at last, and the carriages rolled up to the door to bear the brides and happy grooms away; and as the car- riages whirled down the avenue again they were followed by showers of rice and slippers and the best of wishes of the merry throng that remained at the villa, keeping up the joy and mirth with dancing and revelry far into the night. " My darling—my bride—mine—cc last I' whis- pered Frederick, as he found himself alone will Doris. " Now, from this hour, love, shall our real honeymoon begin," he declared. "I will devote the remainder of my life to make you as hAPPY WI a little queen."

And standing lonely and alone on the deck, the words of the poet occurred to her. Ah ! how true they were—how true! "Two shall be born the whole wide world apart, And speak in different tongues, and have no thought Each of the other's being, and no heed; And these o'er unknown seas to unknown lands Shall cross, escaping wreck, defying death; And all unconsciously shape every act And bend each wandering step to this one end— That one day, out of darkness, they shall meet And read life's meaning in each other's eyes." Vivian avoided them as much as possible on that trip going over, but that, too, was quite a blessing in disguise. What need had a happy bride and groom for the presence of a third party to interrupt their tender love-making? When the steamer landed them on the other side they lost sight of Vivian. Not long afterward they read of her marriage to a duke. The society papers of ter spoke of her after that—of her dresses, her dia- monds' and her cold, proud beauty. She gained for herself the title of " the beautiful icicle.' By that they knew Vivian was not happy. And in truth she was not—she had not married for love. Two years Doris and Frederick spent abroad, and at the end of that time, as Doris declared, Frederick was more of a lover than ever. One sunny morning saw them on board the steamer, bound for " home sweet home." They spent a week at Thornton Villa, then went on to the charming home that had been prepared for them by Frederick's forethought at Cornwall- on-the-Hudson. And there they now live—the happiest couple the sun ever shone on. One of the kindest and noblest acts Doris ever did was, when she heard one day of Madame Delmar's pecuniary troubles, to send her a cheque for an amount which covered her indebtedness. A letter accompanied it, telling Madame Delmar all. The cheque fell from madame's trembling hands to the floor, and her face turned from red to white as she read the letter through, then passod it to her brother John. "If there was ever a case of heaping coals of fire' on one's head, here it is," cried madame, with a burst of tears. "I am glad she bears no ill will towards me." "There are few young girls who would have forgiven you for the way you treated little Doris, and she has repaid you, like the angel she is," said John Delmar, huskily. "Who ever thought in those days that Doris was destined for a great lady ?" she said, slowly. "Treat every one kindly, and yo will never come amiss," replied John. "Are you intending to accept the cheque ?" "1 suppose I must," sobbed ma iame ; "but I shall try to repay Doris some day." Ten years have passed since then; but it does not seem to /lave added a day to Doris's appearan:e, except to expand the gin i into a most gloriously beautiful woman. She is the same Doris as of yore, only her eyes are a deeper blue, the sweet mouth a little more resolute, and her hair has taken on a deeper and more golden sheen, and is ' done up now in a coil more becoming to a wife than the fluffy, golden curls waving about the pretty, dimpled face when we first introduced her to our readers as a school-girl. Mrs. Thornton loves Frederick's wife quite as dearly as her own daughters, all of whom are married now, and are living around her. Madame Delmar still keeps the seminary at Beech Grove for young ladies and misses, an 1 there is a 'room set apart for little lads as well as little lassies. One summer morning a lovely child of, perhaps semi, eight years stands on the seminary steps, with a ronoishi pout on her saucy, red lips, because she has been kept in half of the recess to do her lessons. "If you ask her what her name is she will raise two lovely blue-bells of eyes, and shake back her sunny curls as she answers: "Papa calls me 'pet' and 'little sunshine,' but my mamma calls me Doris Vivian Thornton.' De you see that little boy over yonder, with the wide sailor collar and dark curls? Well, that is my little brother Karl. He is named after my aunt Trixy's husband." Sunshine and shadows cross every household more or less; but taken all in all, it would be difficult to find a happier family than that of Doris and Frederick. What is there to add when those whom we have followed through trials and adversity reach the acme of earthly happiness at last? Re-united after many days, heart to heart and soul to soul, we will leave them, dear reader, these two who were so cruelly parted, almost at the altar.
"Oh, love, if life should be Merely the golden key To love more vast ; If there should be a place Where spirits can embrace, And kisses last."
THE END.

A STRANGE CREMATION.

--- One of the strangest coffins ever told of is one for which the War Office is responsible. The story is that & workman engaged in casting metal for the manufacture of ordnance at the Woolwich Arsenal, lost his balance and fell into a cauldron containing twelve tons of molten steel. The metal was at white heat, and the man was utterly consumed in less time than it takes to tell it. The War Office authorities held a conference, and decidi-d not to profane the dead by using the metal in the manufacture of ordnance, and that mass of metal has actually been buried, and a Church of Eaglami minister read the service for the dead over it.

div.head: I THE WARRINGTON TRAINING
div.p: I THE WARRINGTON TRAINING
COLLEGE..
ANNUAL DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES.

The oistribution of prizes at the Warrington Training College which annually brings together the rektives and friends of the young ladies who are being trained at the Training College as day school teachers,took place 'at the College on Saturday afternoon. The weather was very fine, and as a consequence, there was a good , number present, and the visit was much enjoyed, as the grounds which were thrown open looked at their best. 'the buildings were also open for inspection, and these, especially the new portion aroused a considerable amount of interest.

The task of presenting the prizes was performed by Colonel MORRISON, a member of the Liverpool School Board. and there were also on the platform the Rev. Canon Pet,rhyn, Rev. Canon Willis. Rev. Morley Steven- son, Mr. S. G. Howarth, and Dr. Watkins ; the staff Pre- sent were the Rev. A. B. Hater, Miss Goddard, Miss , 'Perelman, Miss Irna Parkin, Miss Timely, Miss Bate,Mlss Perry, Miss Bell, and Miss Collard. There were also pre- ! sent, Miss Ball, thejlev. B. and Mrs. Percival, the Rev. L. B. Radford, the Rev. G. B. Thurston, Mrs. Stevenson, Mrs. Biter. Mrs. and Miss C:32ton, Mrs. Peurhyn, Mrs. Sharp, Miss White, Miss Lax, Misses Watkins, Dr. arid Mrs. Adams, Mr. and Mrs. MacGregor, Mr., Mrs. and Miss May, Miss Massey, Mr. and Mrs. A." Woods, Mrs. , W. S. Woods,Captain J. D. Buckton. Dr. Guest Gornall, Mr. Isherwood, Captain Royse, R.N., Dr, and Mrs. Shereatt, and about 160 parents and friends of the students at the Institution.

The Principal (the Rev. MORLEY STEVENSON), previous to calling upon Colonel Morrison to distribute the przes, , said that it was customary on occasions like those,to say , a few words before the presentation of the priz,s. He would like, first of all, on behalf of himself, and on be- half of the staff of the college, to offer a very hearty wel- come to all those visitors who bad been kind enough to favour them with their presence that day. They had made a change in the day of prize giving. Formerly they had it on Friday. But that day, as he hoped in future. they would have it on Saturday. That change had been made with the object ot making it more c9nvenient for the parents and friends of the students. He was very anxious that they should regard the prize day to a cer- tain extent, as their day. He was very pleased to see them at least once a year, and %vas very glad that they should have an opportunity of seeing something of the college in which their daughters passed two years of their lives. Ai the prize day would very likely be always in the summer now,they would be able to make it a more plessaut day for them. He was glad to see so many present that day. They would expect him to say some- thing about the work since the last priz3 day, He did not want to weary them with figures and statistics which might be very dry and uniateresting, but he would like them to understand that they had been mak- ing great changes in the college, and there were con- siderable additi. us to it. They would see for themselves, the new part which had been added. He thought they would be able to see that the additions would add very I much to the comfort and efficiency of those living in the college. Ile hoped that they would *lake the collea,s Ira every way, both as regarded the building, the equip- ment, the education given, and4itt was most impor- tant, the moral and spiritual as excellent as any Such college could possibly be made. (Applause.) There were some people who had told him that the students were being made too comtortable, and that such arm- chairs and 3tich couches would not be found even in the homes of the students,and that they were taking a great deal too much trouble in the whole matter. He did not think they had been at all extravagant in the matter. They had done nothing more than was their plain and simple duty. (Applause.) While those young people were there, they were responsible for their health, the brightness and happiness of their lives, and for the in- tellectual atmosphere and culture, and it was the duty of those at the college, to make them comfortable. He must say that he had no sympathy himself with the peo- ple who had every comfort themselves and were always turning up their noses at other people, saying how much too comfortable they were. (Applause.) The past year in the history of the Training College had been an excep- tional one. They had had to get a year's work into half a year owing to the change in the scholastic year, which instead of being from January to December as heretofore, would in future be from July to June. They had had the examinatiori, and whatever the result would be. he thought the students could not be blamed for it. He was glad to say that last year among the second year's students, there was in the certificate examination, not one placed in the third class. (Applause ) This was a very satisfactory result considering that the college was a division college and they were restricted in the one from which the students came. There would be some changes in the' future. It. was thought by many, that the students in training colleges, should be brought as clovly in touch as possible with the Universities, and that the studies should be shaped more nearly to the fashion of the studies in the Universities than they had been in the pact. In Univrrsity towns this could easily be arranged, but they at Warrington were faced with the problem that the College was not in a Universisv town. They had, however, arranged to have professors from the victoria University who were specialists in their studies to come twice a week throughout the term. That was a change which would extail a conshierahle amount of cost upon the college, but which he thought would he, of great benefit to the students. There were some who were widifut to enter for a University course instrai of the ordinary college course. He would, however, warn those who were wishful to do so, that it was necessary to have some previous training. It was compulsory to know Latin,compulsory to know mechanicsond also com- pulsory to take up two other sciences. They would therefore see that it required an education of a much wider and broader character than the ordinary pupil possessed. It would therefore be a great pity to take such a course and fail. Therefore to those who intended to take up this course, he would ask them to prepare for it in good time. With reference to Colonel Morrison, he wasas a lisiast upon the education qaestion. He w known Liverpool for his educational work, welllekant e and had done much good work there.

Colonel MOnstsON, in presenting the prizes, tendered the committee his heartiest thanks for allowing, him to be present that day. He congratulated them upon the alterations which had taken place in the college, which he thought was eminently suitable for the purposes for which it was intended. The whole thing had been done at a moderate cost, the premises costing £3,0a0, and the , whole scheme, including furniture, etc., £41.,500. He was happy to know that the ordinary finances of the college were in an admirable condition. Colonel Morri- son then proceeded to give some good advise to the stndents. He said that it was of the greatest importance that in raqQinz out of that college, they should obtain the first. di vision,as there were many positions thee could net obtain until they were in the first division, and the possibiliges were,that it would be increasingly difficult for the Second division to obtain good positions. Be was pleased to know that out of the 41 appointments of that college, no loss than 37 were to church schools.. lie did not wish to depreciate Board schools,but he thought that the work of the teacher was easier and pleasanter in church schools than in Board schools. He concloded his speech with a tritmte to religious teaching, and argued that this was ho' far the most important. He hamed that the students in their after life would always lay great stress upon that branch of the work and he Wished a successful career to all those who were leaving that year. o,lonet Morrison then proceeded to distribute the prizes which were as follows FIRST YEAR STUDENTS :—Mary Parker, and Christian Stewart, highrst number of marks in all subjects,a writ- ing-case. 'calm 355.; Winifred Algar, Christian Stewart, Mary Trotter, Holy Scripture, the Cambridge Bible commentaries on the four Gospels of the Acts of the Apostles (five volumes) Holy Bible ; Christian Stewart, English literature, composition and history, Milton's Works and Lewis Morris' Poems : Christian Stewart, sohool management, Smith's " Classical Dictionary," Smith's" Dictionary of Antiquities," TAnclora's " Prin- ciples and Practice of Teaching" ; Christian Stewart, domestic. economy and hygiene, Ruskin's "Sesame and Lilies," " Ethics of the Dust," "Queen of the Air" ; Christian Stewart, physiography and geography, " Story of the Heavens," and Ball's " Atlas of Astronomy " ; Mary Parker, arithmetic, Shakespeare's Works ; Mary Parker, French, Lewis Morris' Poems Ruskin's "Sesame and Lilies " ; Florence Burslem needlowork. Shakespeare's Works ; Margaret Webster drawimr., Shakespeare's Works ; Kate Scammell "kangaroo," Tennyson's Poems. • SECOND YEAR' STUDENTS :—Kate Rose, first prize, highest number of marks in all subjects, statiocery cabinet, value £5 ; Emily Plinston,second prize,highest nongher of marks in all snbjects, writing case Melton, Holy Scripture, Keble's " Christian Year Emily Plinston, English literature, and composition, Reql=in'a SC`qAMP and Lilies," " Frondes Agrestes," " Ethics of the Dust " ; Emily Plinston, history and geography. pictures drawn with pen and pencil— England, Scotland, Ireland ; Jane Williams, arthmetic, writing case ; Kate Rose, school management and teach- ;no', Tennyson's Poems ; Kate Rose, domestic economy and brgieno. Longfellow's Poems ; Edith Cooper, Grace Malcolm. needlework. Scott's Poems, Tennyson's Poems; Grace Malcolm, drawing, Shakespeare's Works, and Lewis Morris' Poems ; Era Morton, French, Shakes- peare's Works. and Scott's Poems ; Emily Garlick, general proficiency, selections from Robert Browning's Poems ; Annie Alclernft, the best letter, writing desk. After the presentation had taken place Canon PENRUYN proposed a hearty vat e of thanks to Colonel Morrison for his presence that day. Dr. Wayrxrrss seconded the vote of thanks, and the RECTOR of Warrington, who made his first, public an pearanoe as cawm, supported it. He spoke in high terms of the Principal of the College, and also of the general tone of the students. He wished every success to thate students who were about .to enter upon their duties as elementary teachers. The vote was passed unanimously, and Colonel MORRISON having briefly replied, the meeting termin- ated. Tea was afterwards provided, and the rest of th evening was passed in a pleasant manner in the grounclit:' which adjoined the College. A band was in attendance under tho leadership of Mr. Alfred R. Sutton.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 29 1895.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 29 1895.
WARRINGTON AND THE
GENERAL ELECTION.
MR. A. H. CitOSFIELD'S REPLY.

It will be remembered that a fortnight ago at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the War- rington Liberal Association it was unanimously decided to invite Mr. A. 11. Crosfield to become the Liberal candidate for Warrington at the General Election. It will be learned with regret from the letter which we publish that Mr. Crosfield has, after careful consideration, come to the conclusion that, in view of the state of his health and of th.e claims of his business, he must decline the invita- tion. The following is a copy of the letter :
Walton Lea, near NVarrington, Jane 21st.

Gentlemen,—! write to thank you and equally the members of our Club and party in whose name the proposal was made, for the kind and cordial in- vitation I received a fortnight since, to contest the I Borough in the Liberal interest. I did not feel justified in declining such an in- vitation—unexpected as it was—in any hasty manner, although I felt at that time that it would not be possible for me to accept. -Had circum- stances allowed, I should have been glad to make a fight of it, partly for the saks of old family associations, partly because I do not forget how much we iu the present day owe to Liberalism of the past. With such a duty, it seems mean in an hour of difficulty and possibly temporary defeat, to refuse, any one of us, in what- ever capacity, to put our shoulder to the wheel, in 'support of those, who, like their predecessors, have still to prevent public opinion drifting into a dull and stagnant acquiescence, with all things as they are. _

a.„. But inclination is not enough in such a case. John Bright remarked not many years ago, the modern politician who means to throw his heart into the work, must have a strong stomach for it. lie spoke literally and not figuratively. Without that vulgar hut essential condition,what is to become of the man who rashly courts not merely the extra tax and demand on time and energy, of a political contest, but at least the pos- sibility of a contract between Euston and Bank Quay into the bargain. Ile is no better than a fool rushing in where angels fear to tread. In view, therefore, of a state of health the re- verse'of satisfactory. and the claims—both present and prospective—of my own business, 1 am com- pelled to decline your invitation, while none the less sensible of the honour it confers.

I hope it won't be long before politics in War- rington are of a healthy Liberal complexion,as they ought to be, and again thanking you for an unde- served compliment, remain, faithfully yours. A. H. CROSFIELD.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Musical Society was held the other evening in the Trinity Schools. There was an unusually large attendance of members and officers of the Society, the proceedings being entered upon after a short rehearsal in which both chorus and orchestra took part. Mr. R. T. Fairclough was voted to the chair. Mr. Atkin announced that he had practically no report to submit in his capacity of lion. Secre- , tary, the Society having decided not to give ' any concerts in tlte usual manner during the past season owing to the want of a suitable hall. Nevertheless two concerts bad been given on behalf of the Society as the !result of the enterprise of Mr. Crossley the society's conduc- tor, and Mr. F. W. Reynolds; (applause) and Mr. Lewis Reynolds the Hon. treasurer was pleased to announce that the 'surplus derived from these con- certs along with the members' subscriptions had enabled them to go through the past season's work of continuing the rehearsale,with only a slight loss. The total indebtedness of the society now stood at £79 2s. 93. the gross deficit hav- ing been reduced by a donation of £3l from the Latchford Dramatic Society's performances on be- half of the Society, and by a gift of £1 from a lady member. (Cheers.) Proceeding to the election of officers for the coming year, Mr. Atkin read a letter from Mr. John P.ylands, the President, referring to the pre- sent as being a suitable opportunity of electing a new president, and expressing a desire to retire in favour of the gentleman whose name, had been mentioned as most suitable for the position. On the motion of Mr. Fanshawe it was accordingly unanimously resolved that Mr. J. Charlton Parr be president for the ensuing year, Mr. Rylande' ser- vices in this capacity (luring a long series of years being referred to in felicitous terms. The new vice-presidents are Messrs. R. T. Fair- (dough, John Fairclough, James Fairclough, 11. Garnett, J. H. Gornall, F. Monks, R. Pierpoint, M.P , John White, 5.A. Edelsten, and John Rylands, The old com- mittee were unenimoesly re-elected, and con- sist of Messrs. If. Bond, R. Eccles, D. Fanshawe, H. N. Houghton, .r. Newcombe, P. C. Price. W. Scotson, R. Silcoek, and Herbert Woods. Mr. F. H. Crossley was enthusiastically re-elected as the Society's conductor, Mr. Atkin and Mr. Lewis Rey- nolds were also again asked to take the posts of hon. secretary and hon. sreaeurer, many complimentary references being made to their past arduous services in the interest of the Society. The other officinls re-elected were : Hon.. Librarian, Mr. G. F. F. White ;and Hon. Organist, Mr. J. B. Ca!dwell. The meeting terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

div.head: ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRING-
div.p: ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRING-
TON CHURCH SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Church Society was held on Thursday evening week at the National Schools. In the absence of the President (The Rev. Canon (Willis, the chair was occupied by Mr. C. S. Burgess. There was only a small attendance. The CHAIRMAN regretted that the president was not present that night, as they would have liked to have congratulated him upon the promotion which he had just obtained from the bishop of the diocese. Rethought they had reason to congratulate themselves upon the work of the past session, although they had not realised all the hopes they had formed three years ago. Those who had been responsible for the working of the Society were not to blame for any failure there might have been, however. He hoped the committee which would he elected would he able to introduce a programme which would he attractive as well as instructive,and that they would receive a larger amouot of support from the Church people of Warrington than they had done in the past. Mr. RERI3ERT WOODI, in presenting the third annual report of the Sncietv,said that he must first give expres- sion to the gratification he felt at the distinguished honour that had recently been conferred upon their president, and tenthr him their most hearty congratula- tions. Their work during the year had been confined to two courses of lectures elivered by the Rev. Morley Stevenson. After Christtnas the Rev. H. Gibson Smith gave a course of six lectures on Church 'history up to the Council of Nice. The attendance throughout had been fair and encouraging,vet it was to be regretted that more members had not attended. On March 4, Lord ()IWO presided at a large and enthusiastic meeting held at Warrington in support of the Welsh Church. The committee had resolved to arrange for such a meeting. but when it was found that the ruri-decanal chapter had been arranged for the meeting,it was deemed wiser that the Society should pin with them and abandon its own arrangements. They commenced the year with 87 mem- bers, and during the year there had been 14 new mem- bers. Twa had resigned, and their present membership was 99. Mr. ROBERT DOWON said that the present liability of the Society was £5 is. id, which was lOt. less than

last year. The Secretary's and Treasurer's reports were carried 'unanimously, on the motion of the Rev. Morley Stevens , son seconded by Mr. El. N. Houghton, The following officers were elected : The Rev. Canon Wiliig, president ; Mr. Hestia Art Woods, SPerntary ; Mr. Robert Dobson, treasurer • Recs. Morley Stevenson, W. R. Hartwright, and A. A. Markham, and Messrs. C. 8. Burgess' Captain !Nekton, Appleton, H. J. IVesthroolr..T. riesketh, MacGregor, and D. Banks, committee. Mr. DObßnfi stinested that outing the present year the sub. scription should he doubled in order to pay off the deficit. OF course he would not suErcest that this apply to new members. After Some further discussion upon this point, the meeting terminated.

div.head: WAR itINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: WAR itINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.

A meeting of this Committee was held at the Work- house on Friday. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were present Messrs. T. Halton. J. Billinge. A. Jolley, S. Davies, W. Hickman, J. Clarke' A. J. Jolley, J. Houghton, W. Houghton, G. Pilling ; 3. C. Sutton (clerk),and T. Tunstall (assistant overseer).

. ~ APPEALS BY PUBLICANS. William Berry appealed against the assessment of the "Legh Arms," Newton-le-Willows which was assessed at gross £l3O, rateable £llO 103. on the ground that the takings had fallen off during the last few years. The. privilege of holding picnics on Newton -Lake had been taken away by the lord of the manor,and standing in the fstreets at Newton fair had also been brought to an end, and this it was said, had caused a great difference to the business of the house.—The Clerk said that the landlord was the man who paid the imperial tax. If he didmot choose to allow the appellant so much of the rent as to repay him, the committee could not do anything. All the licensed houses of the Union were now put on the same footing because the coucty rates were now very materially more than they used to he. At the present time the county insisted that the Union should pay upon the imperial tax.—The appellant said that it was not fair that taxation should be increased when the value of the property was being reduced.—The Clerk said that was a matter for the landlord. The present case involved a very important principle.—The appellant complained , that his was the heaviest assessed house in Newton.—Mr. Bdlinge : Have you not the advantage of McCorquodale'S works and Gillespie's works ?—The appellant: They are all women and teetotalers there. When McCorquodale's works are "loosing," I will guarantee that I do not take 6.1.,and there are over 600 people who come out.—The appellant was then asked to retire, and Mr. Owen stated that the house - was purchased for £6,000, but there was no doubt that the business had been reduced considerably.—Mr. Mexicali suggested that the appellant should have an interview with the landlord of UN, ;louse and then come before the Committee again.—The CHAIRMAN asked whether there was much falling off in the receipts of the house.—Mr. OWEN replied that he did not think more than £3O was taken in one,week.—Mr. PILLING and Mr. Elecrod said that the same thing applied to every landlord in the dis- trict, and the former moved that the assessment remain as 7:t was. He thought that if they allowed ad abate- ment in one case, they would have a lot of trouble as there would be appeals all round. He also thought that the house was assessed to a reasonable amount.—Mr. A. J. JOLLEY seconded the motion which was passed unani- mously.—Mr. Berry was then called in and informed of the decision of the Committee.—The CHAIRMAN sug- gested that he should see his landlord and persuade him to appeal to the income tax commissioners against the assessment. As long as the landlord was content to pay taxes on £l3O, the Committee could not see their way to put the assessment below what was required by the county. James Worrall, beer-house keeper, 2 Pitt-st., Warring- ton, also appealed against the assessment of his house at £6O. He said that an hotel had been built near his house and had taken away a lot of his business.—Mr. WILLIAM HotrouToie : The people at the hotel complain that you have taken away their business. (Laught ). —Mr. OWEN said that the assessment of the ho u ,s„ ha.: ~ .‘o doubled. —The CLERK in explaining the caaan (.. r tie, increased assessment,said that the tendency in Warrington was to reduce public-houses, not to increase them, although the population was increasing. It would consequently cause an increase in the value of the houses. The Com- mittee had to pay the county rat( which were fixed upon the houses, and if the house were assessed by the Committee at a lower figure than by the income tax commissioners, it would practically amount to the fact that ether ratepayers would have to pay paak of the rates of the hou . . The only plan would be for the landlord of th ouse, Mr. Bolton, to endeavour to get his assessor. •.7 the commissioners reduced, and then .1 the assessmea 'mid come down all round.—The Com- mittee decided not to allow the appeal, and the aepel- ant on going out said that it was very hard, as he could I carcely make a living.

Miss Harriet A. Wright and MiS3 Mabel Wright, daughters of Mr. George Wright, of Heysham Lodge, near Morecambe, were drowned while bathing in Heys- ham Bay on Monday. An adjourned inquest regarding the death of five women owing to a boiler explosion on May 23 on the Premises of Mr. John Shaw, woollen manufacturer, Beestows Mill,Stainland,was ccncluded on Monday. Mr. John Wa ugh, of Bradford, reported that the explosion was attri hatable to the worn-out condition of the boiler. The jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against Mr. Shaw. Pending police proceedings,the Coroner admitted Mr. Shaw to bail in his own recognisauces of £2OO and two sureties of £lOO e ach.
THE CHARGE OF EMBEZZLENIENT AGAINST A BRANCH AIANAGER.
COMMITTAL f 0 PRISON.

At the Warrington Borough Plies Court on Tues- day morning, beiore Mr. R. Garnett (chairman), Dr. T. S. Smith and Counciilor Roberts, Frank Garrett w.s charged that he on the 22nd December, 1894, being in the service cf John Ffarrop, 55, Tibh-st., Manchester,did feloniously embezzle and steal 24 2s. and within six cal- ender months thereof divers other sums to wit in January 18,,t £1 15e. and on 13..11 April £3. A 9 in the previous hearing of the case prisoner was represented by Mr. Percy Davies, and the case for the prosecution was taken by Mr. Browne. Mr. Browne said that his client, Mr. Flarrop, of 55 Tibb•stre.et, Manchester, was a cabinet malt-ir in a large way, having different branches in certain towns, one of them being in Bridge-street,Warrington, and the prisoner was manager m that branch. His duties were as follows: —He was to take orders, sell goods, receive money, and weekly to pay that money in the bank, and the amount which he paid into the bank must app-ar on the "sub- scription "lists which were forwarded to the head office in Manchester, so that the money in the bank must correspond with the money on the list, otherwise there would have been suspicions aroused at once and which might have resulted in the present proceedings at an earlier date. In this case it was not the ordinary one of
receiving money, putting it down and not accounting for it. - - - -

Mr. Garnett (interrupting) : Is he responsible for the balance of the money over and above his expenses. Mr. Browne: Yes sir. He was allowed to take out shop expenses but the balance must agree with his book. The first case, he said, was tat of Mr. Frank Hawthorn- waite, a wiredrawer at Smith's works, Dallam-lane. In June of last year he was engaged to be married in August. He saw Mr. Garratt and told him that he would like to have some furniture from them and would bring his wife to choose the furniture and he arranged with Mr. Garratt to go on paying, in other words he would pay to the firm certain sums of money from time to time on account of his furniture. Mrs. Hawthorn- thwaite, then single, went with him and pick NI out goods to the amount of £22 in July and asked Mr. Garratt to put them on one side and Mr. Hawthorn- thwaite would go on paying for the goods until they had a house to remove them to when they were married. The prisoner did se and they paid several sums of money but unfortunately were prevented from being married in August and until December when they had. paid ..£ll.

73.61 The goods were delivered that month by Mr. Garratt who gave Lia wthornthwaite a fresh book and at the same time he pot 10i. at the top. They went on paying on th it book with the 103. at the top until the 18th of March. The 4 T. 61. was not there at all but in another book. Atte/ this the prisoner saw Mr. Havrthornthwaite and told. hinil there was some
arrear in their books and asked for the old book in order that they might rectify it. Mr. tiawthornthwaite ob- jected b,t Mr. Garratt said he would give him a clnu- __. . .
ment and thereupon put the 103. on the ton,of the book. They noticed afterwards that there was 59. 61 put be- tween the lines which Mr. flawshorntliwaite and his

wife had never paid. That 153. fid. taken off the £4 7s. 6d. left the sum of £3 12. The 103. was part of this and had therefore been accounted for. Before Mr. Hawthornthwaite would part with the old book Mr. Garratt gave him this :—" Bridge-st., 113th June. I owe you £3 12 i.to be brought with book when settling."—F. Garratt. Instead of this document being given on June 18' h it was given on March 23rd of the present year, 8 or nine months after Mr. GArratt had been receiving the money. Mr. Browne's instructions were that Mr. Oar- ratt had no authority to do tins whatever. There still remained the £3 12s. mentioned in the 1.0. U. t,) ac- . .

counted for. Mr. Garratt had called on Hawthorn- thwaites on the Friday before Whit Sunday to see whether the dresser had been repaired. This was after he had left the Warrington branch. Mrs. Haw thorn- thwaite had seen the present manager and he had offered to change it for her. Garrett asked her " Has anyone told anything to you aboot this book," and she replied " No." He saw the 1.0. U. in sh, book and took it out and then asked that it shoald be kept out until they had nearly paid up the £22. He handed it to her and she afterwards named it to her husband who accom- I panied her to the shop, and it was then discovered that it hid never been accounted for. In consequence of this Mr. Flarrop instructed Mr. Browns to take proceed- ings. His client's object was not revenge but as a de- terrent to the large number of other men in his employ. If prisoner pleaded guilty to the charge cortnec'el with Hewthernthwaite Mr. Browne was prepared to with- draw the other charges arid let the matter end there. He threw that out as a suggestion. Mr. Davies said that under the circumstances and on behalf of the prisoner he pleaded guilty to the charge of Hawthornthwaite's matter. He applied for Mr. Browne's permission to ask Mr. Hawthornthwaite a question. Mr. Browne consented, and Mr. Davies asked him when he first found out that the document was an 1.0. U. Witness replied that he and his wife did not know what it was at the time hut thought it was a receipt. They discovered its real nature about a fortnight after. Mr. Davies said that as an advocate he felt his position keenly. He had taken a course which he had doubts as to whether he ought to have taken or not. He hoped they would agree with him that he had taken a wise course in pleading guilty to the first charge. The prisoner,he said, had never been in a police court before and was there- fore a first offender. He had been in a most responsible position for four years and had most extraordinary au- thority. Here was a man, he submitted, who had the very fullest authority almost to do anything and it was almost impossible for him to carry out the dutiee which he had to carry out without getting, into a muddle He received from 600 to 800 accounts a week and nowhere to put the money except in his pocket. There was no till on the premises. Mr. Browne There was a safe. Mr. Davies : If there is another business house in Warrington withant a till I'll eat it. Mr, Garnett : There is no till its our Mile., Mr. Davies : I never knew a cashiers' office without a till in my life. Continuing, he submitted that it would be impossible if it was true that there were 800 accounts a week to which he attended himself and was respensible. for him to attend properly to the work. During the 4 I years he was in this employment he had a sick wife who was not expected to live and prisoner was forced to I borrow money. On the b,,,h of March he received the ' following letter from his employer " Dear sir, I must ask you to take a week's notice commencing from the day your successor will commence his duties of manager and you will be requested to initiate him in the werk I will find you an engagement in Mr. Shore's Depart ment. I believe a change in Warrington would be better for both ot us—Yours truly, John Herron." Prisoner went to this situation and was pounced upon by a very 1 respectable gentleman—Detective Monaghan—and put in durance vile, locked up without bail and had been without bail ever since he came because the amount which was settled upon for sureties made it impassible for prisoner to get it. Mr. Davies ssid that taking into con- sideration the amount of work prisoner had to do, the amount of money he had for doing it-30s. a week.— Mr. Browne: 355., house, coal and gas. Mr. Davies : Thirty and no more. All they knew was that he had never received more than 30s. Prisoner here informed his solicitor that he received in addition the house and lights. Mr. Davies then referred back to the number of accounts prisoner had to &el with in the week, when Mr. Bowne interrupted and said that there had been 675 payments in four years. A book of receipts was then handed to the Bench and Mr. Garnett said the number came down to about 60 accounts a week. Councillor Roberts asked whether the man had been ! anything like adequately paid for the responsibility of his position. If he had not it was a temptation; if he had it was a serious matter. This question was answered by the accounts been passed up to the Bench for private consideration. Mr. Davies observed that he said it advisedly he would have fought the case if it had not been that they would have had to wait three weeks, because he did not believe the impossible statement about the 1.0. U. They were asked co believe that a man received an 1.0. U. and did not know what it was. The macistrates expreised themselves as being quite satisfied with the evidence of the witness Hawthorn- waite. Continuing, Mr. Davies said it Should be taken into consideration that it was prisoner's first case and that he had a sick wife ; his previous good character and multifarious duties and especially his having a sick home and that he had been very severely punished by being in prison ever since. They could deal with him under the first offender's act. Mr. Browns: That cannot be done. Mr. Davies :I am very sorry I have had such difficul- ties all round. Mr. Browne: It is not right to say that. I have done all I could for your help consistent with my duty. He added that they did not want to press the case but only to make it a deterrent example. After an interval during which the Bench considered their decision Mr. Garnett said they had very carefully discuseed the case and tried to give the kindliest view to it and he Was not sure they were absolutely just because the law looked upon defalcation of this kind very severely, and he had not the slightest doubt that if the case bad cone for trial the prisoner would have met witb a very severe punishment. His counsel had acted wisely in pleading guilty in the first charge. There was no doubt the prisoner had been led to appropriate the monies, and there was also no doubt that the position in which he had been was a very responsible one, but he was bound to he honest. Mr. Garnett said he made these remarks in the hope that they would be of some service to him in the future. Taking a most lenient view of the case they had come to the conclusion that it would be met by sen- tencing prisoner to 14 days imprisonment without hard labour. Mr. Garnett then added that it was very good of the prosecution to deal as favourably with prisoner as they could.
