div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
CYCLING.

On the Fallowfield track on Sdurday,Mr.J. Wadding- ton, of ‘Varrington, was fourth in the 12 hours' path race held by the Manchester Wheelers. Rosser of Swan- sea, was first with 242 miles and 2 laps, Waddington's distance being 224 miles, 1,500 yards.

div.head: SWIAtMIMG.
div.p: SWIAtMIMG.

In the Liverpool and District Water Polo League, the Warrington team is now looked upon as one whi,ih it is an honour to conquer. Their remarkable success in the competition last year won them a name, while this sea- son they have won every match, and with some sub, stantial majorities. Their surprising success against Sefton on Tuesday night placed them in the enviable position of being at the top of the League table, a place which they have a good chance of hoLiing, provided that the St. Helens team can also be persuaded to" bite the dust,"—or more correctly, "the water." this team is also playing well, and being the winners of last year the first meeting of the two teams will be looked forward to with more than ordinary interest.

The next engagement whine the Warringtonians have is with the Liverpool Diamond T, at Liverpool. These "jewels" are also in fair form, but as in their last match they only drew with Sefton, their chances are not of the brightest,notwithstanding that they stand second in the LeAgue.

Tuesday night's match was one-sided as regards scor- ing, but not in acted play. The Seftoraians proved themselves exceptionally strong swimmers. and a very hot contest was the result. Locker, Scotson, Beaman, and Ashton played in first-class form for the home team, while Proctor, Finnigan. and Rose were also very ener- getic on the opposite side. Fouling was a little too fre- quent,but was afterwards a.2counted for by a misunder- standing which had arisen through the erroneous idea getting abroad that Sefton were going to appeal against the previous match. At the supper table, when all hos- tilities were merged into friendliness, this was fully ex- plained by the Sefton captain.

It would be a good thing for all concerned if W. Sutton could be persuaded to enter the lists again as a first team player. His capabilities were clearly shown last year, and further evidence was provided in his strong play while forward in the Reserve team match with Widnes this year.

This event was the direct opposite of the League match and the Widnes, players were sadly deficient in both swinaming and shooting. The Reserve men proved th,rnselves unusually strong in these points,as their win of 10 goals to nil amply shows.
Chemicals are evidently poor material for athletic training.
CRICKET.

Warrington are improving, and following their victory over Oldham, they pulverised Preston on Saturday, and atoned for the defeat they Buffered on May 4th at the hands of this club. The win was no fluke either, for those who saw Wsrrington, aver that never before had they fielded so well, and they were also greatly superior with both bat and ball. The victory wag in fact well earned, and will greatly inspire the Warrington team.

Mr. S. M. Crosfield made a welcome reappearance in the team at the match, this being his first match this season, and he quickly showed that he was in form, for his partnership with George Clarke was the most attrac- tive part of the match. R. Smith and J. J. Crosfield gave their side a very good start with 69 and 63 respectively, and S. M. Crosfield and G. Clarke made the highly respectable scares of 24 and 23,and these with 15 extras, and a few minor scores brought the total to 206. The formidable task of passing this was quite above the ability of Preston who had to be content with 101.-

Smith who was top scorer for Warrington was also the most destructive bowler, taking five wickets for 27 runs. Connor also took three for 35, and J. J. Crosfield two for 24, It was a source of great satisfaction to Warrington when" Jimmy" Ross was clean bowled by his friend Connor for only four runs, as the association football player contributed largely to the defeat of Warrington at the first meeting.

The Liverpool team were encountered on Wednesday but before the match had been long in progress, the thunderstorm came'on, and the game was obandoned. Warrington were therefore robbed of an opportunity of avenging their first defeat at the hands "t Liverpool, as they had a reasonable hope of ding as they had a very strong team.
The followinz are the averages of the Warrington players up to date. It will be noticed that J. J. Cros- field has come up with a bound, and has scored his 100 11.1116
times Innings not out runs R. Smith 6 . 0 J J. Crosfleld Bites W It Poimore . 5 Clark (A) 7 G Clarke J Callon 8 B Boglancl W Wordiworth . 6 ' . 0 B uonnor

The second team met Go!borne on Saturday for the third time this season. On the first two occasions, neither could beat the other, bot the teams managed to come to a definite conclusion this time, though it was not satisfactory from a Warrington point of view, for Go!borne won bv 138 to 128. C. H. Unsworth, the local secretary, helped the Golhorne team, and he was unkind enough to knock up 36, the highest Golhorne score. Bibby as usual was the top scorer for Warrington with 39. If the second do not bestir themselves, the first will have a better record than they.

The Sankey Wesleyans, first and second, were victori- ous on Saturday, each winning decisively. The victim; were Bedford Leigh Wesleyans, first and second. Bed- ford first, who fought on their own ground,put together the respectable figure of 51. The Sankey Wesleyans' innings was a curiosity. Only five men batted, and three of these made "ducks," yet the remaining two made moo than tke eleven of their opponents. This distinguished pair were Clare and Booth, who scored 19, and 33 r?spectively. Three bowlers were required to diamisa Bedford, viz., Pownalt 2 for 2, Llewellyn 4 for 18, and Watkins 2 for 22. The victory of the second team was largely due to J. Tonge, who put on 17 in double quick time. J. Roderick had a good bowling analysis of 7 for 14, his brother bowler Cotterall taking tha remaining wickets for 16 runs.

The Sankey Wire Mills first and second were opposed to C.L.C. Engineers, first and second, on Saturday, and while the first lost by two rum, the second won by the same number, thus counterbilincing matters a little. Both matches were productive of low scoring, Simpson being the highest scorer in the first for Sankey with 10, and Howard for C L.C.with 12. Oaly one player in the second teams reached double figures, and that was Higham. who scored 12 for the Engineers.

The Penk4th Weslenans and the Penketh Cabinet Works eng,Aged ha friendly combat on Sitnrciay,and the former won easily by an innings and 17 runs. The strength of the Wesleyans lay in their bowling, and this more than their batting contributed to their vic- tory.

I notice that Peter Walker and Sons 2nd had to eat humble pie on Saturday, and that the Grammar School have proved the better of them. They have been so accustomed to victory that it will la, a new experience for them to be beaten. Basn.tt C.C. evidently over- estimated the strength of St. Paul's, for they did not close their innings on Saturday until they had scorrd 100 for the loss of six wickets, Dooley being then 51 not out. St. Paul's had lost five wickets for six runs when time arrived, and saved them from an ignominous defeat. They did not pass a vote of thanks to old Father rime for it,however. The Y. M.G. A. also had the unusual ex- perience of defeat on Saturday, Aston Hall school being stronger by 93 to 52 Picton (22), and Sanders (10) were the only Y.M.C..A. players to make a stand.

Lancashire have revenged their two defeats at the hands of Kent last year, by beating the hop county twice this year. Theuah not quite to decisive as the first victory, the victory on Saturday was net a narrow one. Briggs for a change had the best bowling average at this match. Lancashire have still the best relative position, but as a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush, Surrey on this principle are the best off for the championship, for they have a lead of three points over Lancashire with four matches more played.

W. G. Grace has scarcely allowed a werk to pass since the season began without scoring a century, and he has just managed to accomplish this, this week hi• scoring 101 for the Gentlemen of Ragland against the Zingari.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at Bowspy Crfamty.rs on W.thlesiity, the ChAirman being the Rev. G. F. R)herts, and there were 4130 present. M-ssrs. W. Houpton, J. Houghton, T Halton, J. W. Knowles; S. Str.ton (clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), and F. Kerfoot (nuisance imsnctor).

FINANCIAL MATTERS. The CLERK sij that th, aknee au the hands of the treasurer was £99 104. 8,1. on the general account, £1 900 154., on flys Burton wood sewage account, and £B3 7s. 81. on the Rixton sanitary loan account.

THE POWER OF DEALING WITH OFFENSIVE TRADES. The CLERK real letter Iron the Local Goverment Board in reply to aa app!icalon to confer upon the Council powers to deal with offensive tm les in the dis- trict, to the effect that section 112 of the Public Health Act of 1875 oid not confer upon the Rural District Council the I:,nwer to deal wi`h off.nsive trades in their district. The B wished to know whether under Oe circumstances Ow Cannell still desired the powers, Thfy PASO wished to know wh.ohe:. Viet: .unc.l desired to have the powers of sections 113 and 114. of the Act. These seetions would not give them the power to deal with existing offensive trades, but would in ca.se of trades which miqiit be introduced in future —The CHAIRMAN said that it was deshable that they should have this power, and it was decided to make noplication for it.
EXTENSION OF THE BOROUGH OF %FARRINGTON.

Board informing the Council that the apolication for the extenmion of the tyirough had been granted. The Clerk said that the Town Clerk of Warrington hal expre,owd his willingness to take over the liabitities of the portions in the distrot of the Council. MITCLIELL. A letter was read from the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, vicar of flintenwood, as fellows :—'• St. Michael's Vicarage. Buttonwood, Jun' 7.h. Dear sir,—You wrote to me, I bAteve, whilst I was ill, about the outlet from our cess- pool, but your letter cannot at present be found. The Authority requires me to close up the outlet into the ad- joinina (+itch. It is roasenable to ask if the same re- qeirernent has hen laid upon the owners of all the dwelling-houses in this neighbourhood. Ditches and filthy ponds are freely used for sewstze purposes. If ou do not need of course to he reminded of the deplorable neglect of the Sanitary Authority in this parish, as the result of which Burton wood is to-day, in parts no better than a cesspool. Nor can you be ignorant of the fact that the Medical Officer of Health is in this locality an imaginary being.iand not a living personality. (Laugh- ter.) The new Council whitih has now taken up the work fsf the Saul; ary Authority requests me to do m 9 own Sanitary work, and at the same time to pay for the sanitation of other people—in fact to pay for a wealthy colliery company. You are, however, apparently in ignorance of the fact, that if the outlet of which yon complain (and I do not justify the outlet) is closed, the Authority is responsible for the emptying of the ce3s- I pool, and this I would have to ask you to do twice a week • Yeu will I think find that I am correct. Any person of ordinary intelligence and unbiassed mini can see that the Authority is only trang with a serious mater, and that the sooner you provide a proper sewer the better. If you persist in your foolish policy ef ob- struction, and refuse to extend the sower already laid down, I believe in Alder-Line, or connect us with the new sewage works near at hand, I most exercise the privilege of a principal householder of appealing to the Local Government Board for Inquiry. The Authority will be aware that the very hot weather is very prejudi- Mai to the heath of our people, in consequence of the in- sanitary state of things. My own attack of diphtheria is to be laid at the iiaor of your Council." Mr.Witaaasi Flouoarov : He does not claim damages. (Laughter.)—The C tairman : What has the medical officer to say to this charge P—the Nuisance Inspector I appear to have escaped this tiine.—The Medical Offler : I am afraid I have been too severe with him.— me Knowles : But he says he never sees you—Toe Medical Officer: I will have to go and have a glass of wine with him whenever Igo in that district. (Laugh. ter.)—The Clerk said that the Council had not the privilege of seeing the plans of the house when it was being built, or of passing any opinion upon them. When the copies of the plans were asked tor, they were in- formed that it was unnecessary as it was a matter for the Ecclesiastical Commis ioners. It was found that under these circumstances the S nit try Au'hority had no power. It was a cesspool from Mr. Mitchell's house that ran into the ditch.—The Chairman wished to know under what power the Ecclesiastical Commissioners were exempt.—The Clerk said that it was under similar circumstances as.harracks and county constabularies._ In reply to Mr. Knowles, Mr. Kerfuet said that the ditch was on the highroad by the side a the vicarage.-- Mr. Knowles said that in a case in which be was in- velved, it was held that on a highroad, the property- owner owned four feet from the boundary fence. It wart therefore clear that Mr. Mitchell was responsible for the state of the ditch.—Toe nuisance inspector was in- structed to proceed in the usual manner in this case. proceedings had previously been postponed owing to Mr. Mitchell's illness.

The vacant places of Greater Warrington will, it is to be hoped, soon be iilledup with works and dwelling houses, with re- creation grounds here and there for the health and enjoy ment of a growing population. Cromwell has been very much es evidence during the past fortnight, and the most conflicting opin- ions have been advanced respecting him. It is wonderful to what extent the remembrance of his name has been kept all over the British Isles. If a castle is in ruins, it is, of course, Oliver Cromwell who knocked it down, and if any bullets or cannon balls are discovered, they must have been shot out of some of Cromwell's cannons or guns. The mem- bers of the Warrington Highway Board had on view at their last meeting,a cannon ball, and bullet, and the opinion was at once expressed that they were Cromwellian. Mr. Matthews suggested them as suitable presents for the Irish members, who have taken so prominent part in opposing the erection ot a statue of Cromwell by the Government. It is, however, much more probable that these relics 'will find their way to the Warrington Museum.

1 Everyone was pleased with the success which attended the Warrington Y.M.C.A. garden party held at Walton Lea. In addition to the very pleasant games which were provided, at the tea table there was some speechmaking of an interest- ing nature. The. Rev. E. T. Reed explained the origin, value, and objects of the Association in a most lucid manner, while Mr. A. 11. Crosfleld and other speakers contrived to infuse not a little humour into their speeches. The host's kindness was warmly appreciated and this visit to Walton Lea will be remembered with pleasure by all who took part in it.

div.head: WATER POLO AT WARRINUTON.
div.p: WATER POLO AT WARRINUTON.

The close proximity of Walking Day had, no doubt, something to do with the poor attendance at the War- ringt n Baths on Tuesday evening. There was not a full gala programme but with the reduced admission charges the items provided were sufficiently attractive to justify the appearance of a crowded attendance. Mr. J. Grace acted as stater in the club handicap and the polo referee was Mr. Nevins, of Liverpool. Mr. D. Walsh, hon. sec. of the Warrington Swimming Club was al:o present. In the final of the 50 yard's club handicAp the com- petitors were L. Davies, C. Ashton, M. Walker. Graham and Thompson. The race was warmly contested and resulted in Davies being first, Gramm second, and Ashten third. A flying squadron race between the Widnes and Warrington reserve teams was the next item, the teams being as follows :—Warrington—Creig- ton, Wright, Jones, Walsh, and Ashton ; Widnes— Robinson, Flurstfield, Owen, Bruce, Lloyd, and Benbow. Of the six heats Warrington won five with little difficulty. Following this came the first polo match between the Widnes team and Warrington Reserve. A more amusing display of polo could hardly be found than that afforded by the half-hearted play which char- acterised the Widnesians, who were quite out-played and hnable to score a single goal. On the other hand the Warrington Reserve team proved themselves quite adepts in the game, the majority of them being good shooters with the ball which they put through their Opponents' goal posts ten times during the match. Eight were shot in the first half and two in the second. The scorers were : Wright, 3 ; Sutton, 3 ; Walsh, 1 ; Jones, 1 ; Clough, 1 ; and Creighton. 1. Some of these were taken at long range, and one shot from Sutton was rendered successful by the Widnes goalkeeper catch- ing the ball but clumsily knocking it behind his .posts..

The next and final event was the return match b-t- -ween Warrington and Sefton, in the Liverpool and Dis- trict League. The teams were strongly made up by— Warrington : Dixon, goal ; Beaman and Furness, full backs ; Scotson, half-hack ; Locker (centre), Turner and Ashton, forwards ; Sefton : Wilson, goal ; Rose and Smith,full backs ; Finnigan,half-hack ; Proctor (centre), Spratt and Parry, forwards. In the first half of the ganae Sefton, winning the toss, defended the deep end of the bath, and on the throw out Locker was first to the hall, and getting towards the front essayed a shot which to the surprise of all went through the Sefton goal in a trice. After the restart when Locker was again and ever after first to secure, Ashton came in possession and passing back to Scotson,the latter scored the second goal. Turner had the next opporturnty and sent in a couple of "stin- gers "in rapid succession, hut the attempts were re- pulsed, until Beaman followed the example of his prede- cessors by planting another goal. Some diimay was manifest among the Seftonians at this, and they accord- ingly played for all they were worth, making the game more even and allowing Proctor to make an ineffectual shot: This, however, gave little relief, and a moment- later Ashton seizing the ball and spying a clear route swam to within a yard or en of his opponents' gral and neatly notched another point. Locker next passed to Scritson who put in one of his three-quarter bath shots and was within an ace of scoring. Sefton were favoured by a goal throw from this and succeeded in temporarily relieving the pressure, which was further stayed by Fin- nigan, being fouled by Scotsnn. Nothing waslproductive of the relief, however, and the game once more pro- gressed in favour of Warrington who through Locker's instrumentality scored a goal. Another series of fouls ensued from which Ashton broke away, and shot the sixth goal for the homesters. This saw the advent of half time, with Warrington lead- ing by 6 goals to nil. On getting off in the second portion of the match Sefton were seen to decided advantage, with the shallow end of the bath in their favour. More shot e than one were sent into Dixon's hands. while the fouls which were perpetrated led the refereeto order Locker out of the bath. This was happily taken in good part by the spectators, while the Warrington captain's loss was at once apparent, the Sefton forwards having it all their own way. A anal throw came as a god-send for War- rington. and for this Beaman was applauded for another goal. This event re-instated Locker, andthe game was reversed, 00(101 Rose, of Sefton, was enabled to score the only goal for the( viftitnrs. Seritson put in a number of tiemendeua throws, one of which succeeded in pas- sing the &Ron goal. Little was done by either side in the ensuing few minutes of play, which ceased at the call of time with Warri agton winning a hard-fought game by 8 goals to Sefton 1. This success exceeded that of the previous week with th,. same team, when to Warringtnn's 8 Sefton opposed 3, and at the same time Tuesday's victory raised the home tram one point ahead of th. Liverpool Diamond T team, and thus at the top of the League. After the match the visitor; were treated to an excel- lent supper at t e Baths Hotel, when the healths of each team and its captain were drunk with enthusiasm. o!her toasts were also honoured, and an hour of con- viviality pleasantly spent.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 29 1895
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 29 1895
RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

THE SHIPMENTS OF SALT AT RUNCORN. The returns of the shipments of salt at Runcorn and Weston Point for last week proved exceptionally satis- factory. They are the largest known for some time, al- though of late the figures have been considerably increased. The tonnage of white salt was 8,080, and of rock salt, 870 tons. The steamer Rose, from Manches- ter, is now lying, at Saltport, taking in a cargo cf 1,000 tons of salt for the Baltic.

GARDEN ROBBERIES AT RUNCORN. , At Runcorn Police Court on Friday morning, before Mr. John Brundrit, a charge of stealing 24 geranium plants and six calceolaria plants of the value of 10s. was preferred against a middle-aged woman named Elizabeth Morgan, of no fixed abode. It was alleged that the plants were taken from the garden of Mr. William Mel- lor, Stanley Villas, Higher Runcorn, between 10 p.m. on the 18th aud 6 a.m. on the 19th inst.—After a cood deal of evidence had been given, the magistrates committed the accused to prison for one month. Sr. JOHN BAPTIST SCHOOL, WESTON. Is St. Edward's Romani Catholic Church on Sunday, July 71h, the annual sermons on behalf of St. John Baptist School, Weston, will be preached by the Rev. Father Byrne, B.A. Reference will be made to the , recent objections to the re-union of the Christian Churches, at the evening service. The services will commence at 11 a.m. and 630 p.m. SUDDEN DEATH OP A WELL-KNOWN RUNCORN CAPTAIN. On Wednesday, the death occurred somewhat sud- denly, of Captain Thomas Foster, residing at 30, Elias- mere-street,Runcorn. The deceased who was 53 years of age. was taken ill on Tuesday and was attended by Dr. Robinson who has certified death to be due to "heat-apo- plexy." He had been a captain for about 30 years and had been largely connected with the coasting trade. Since tie opening of the Manchester Ship Canal he had acted as pilot, and he assisted to navigate the first vessel to Manchester. He was widely known and leaves a widow, two daughters and a son to mourn his loss. BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. This Sunday school will celebrate its 95th anniversary on Sunday, and the preacher engaged for the occasion is the Rev. S. Chadwick, of the Leeds Mission. Mr. Chad- wick has established most successful missions in Edin- burgh, Leeds. and London, and he ranks with the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes as the most effective speaker in Methodism.. He will preach morning and evening in St. Paul's Wesleyan Church' and on Monday evening, in the same edifice, he will deliver an address on a subject which should arouse no small amount of curiosity, entitled "Sixes and Sevens." On this Occasion Coun- cillor Collier' whose brother's mission work in Man- chester is well-known, will make his first appearance in public in the role of chairman. The proceedings will commence at seven o'clock. Collections will be taken on behalf of the school funds, and as the school is Vie largest in the town liberal assistance is asked for. AN ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN. A married man named Samuel Glover, of Salkeld- square, Runcorn, was brought before Messrs. J. lmison, at Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday morning, for attempting to commit suicide on the 24th inst.—P.C. Booth stated that at 3.30 on Monday afternoon from Information received he went to the prisoner's house. He found that the door was lacked and he forced it open. On going into the back room he saw the prisoner with a knife in his hand. Widness immediately went up to him, knocked him on the ground, and took the knife from him. Prisoner bad already made a cut in his throat about 14 inches long, but not very deep.—ln- speetor Hicks thought the prisoner should be remanded to linutsford Gaol until Monday in order that a doctor might examine him.—The magistrates agreed with this, and accordingly remanded the prisoner. FLOWER SERVICE AT THE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. There were good congregations at the annual flower services held in Bethesda Congregational Church en Suu- day. The pulpit and communists rails were very prettily decorated with a profusion of plants and flowers. The former were kindly lent by Mrs. Haziehurst, The Grange, and flowers were contributed by Mr. Roberts, Mrs. Stormont, Miss Richardson, Mrs. Morris, Mrs. Chamberlain, Mr. J. Lunt, Mr. W. Cooke, Mrs. Temple, Mrs. Davies, Mrs. France, Mrs. Elliott, Mrs. Taylor, Miss Slade, Mr. T. Lunt, Mrs. Ryder. Dr. Robinson, and others. The work Wag performed by Misses Robb, Heatherington, Cringball, Richardson, Stone, Slade, Abrams, and Entwistle. At the evening service the pastor, the Rev. J. Simpson, preached on " the Garden of Life." Solos were effectively sung by Mrs.Temperley and Mr. C. Leathweod and the choir interpreted with precision the anthems " Rejoice, rejoice," and " 0 taste and see." Mr. le Ceuteur officiated at the organ. A RUNCORN Lan SENT TO A REFORMATORY. At Runcorn Police Court on Thursday morning before Mr. Thomas Handley (chairman), and Mr. E. unison, two lads named Martin Gilligan, 14 years of age, and Daniel Cain, 11 years of age, were charged with break- ing and entering the rope works of the Manchester Ship Canal Company with intent to commit a felony at 645 the previous evening. Both lads pleaded not guilty to the charge, stating that they went there to shelter from I the rain and not with the intentien of stealing anything. , —Mr. William Henry Chadwick, manager of the ;emery, Said from information received from Mr. William Hewitt of Percival-lane, he proceeded to the works about 6.30 the previous night. He found one of the doors had been opened and on going inside the works he saw the two prisoners. He watched them for a short time,and eventually with the assistance of ter. Hewitt he caught them. On looking round the works that morning he found a small quantity of ends of rope had been put at the bottom end of the works ready for carrying away. He left the works locked up for the night. The prisoners must have got over the will in Percival-lane and then got in at the top end of the Ropery. His suspicious had been aroused by missing several things. One of the men had had a jacket st.ilen, another a can, and be had missed several iron Isare.—William Hewitt said he saw the prisoner Cain climb over the wall just past the engine house and the other one got over lower down.— P.C. Butler also gave evidence, and Superintendent Hicks described Cain as a complete nuisance. He had been before the magistrates many times, and his father was being continually summoned for the lad's irregular school attendance. The last time lie was before the magistrates, he was birched for stealing a sovereign. He thought a reformatery was the best place for hirn.—The magistrates fined Gilligan, who bore a better character, 2s. 6d. including costs, and ordered Cain to a reforma- tory for five years. WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS. We would draw our readers' attention to the annual Widnes Athletic Club Sports which will be held at the Sports Field, Parnworth, Widnes, on Friday and Saturday, July 12th and 13th. A large number of valuable prizes will be completed for,the events including 1,000 yards scratch,flat and bicycle race handicaps. A very interesting event will be the five mile championship contest, of the Widnes Cycle Club. All intending competitors should enter for the events at the earliest opportunity, as the entries close on July 6th. For the convenience of intending visitors, special trains will be run from Warrington. Liverpool, and Manchester via the C.L.C. at reduced fares.

div.head: QUARTERLY MEETING OF THE RUNCORN WESLEYAN
div.p: QUARTERLY MEETING OF THE RUNCORN WESLEYAN

CIRCUIT. In Brunswick Vestry on Monday evening the quarterly meeting of the Runcorn Wesleyan circuit was held for the trounae, ion of the usual business. There was a large attendance of representatives. Tea was provided when the tables were presided over by the following ladies : Mrs. Brackenbury, Mrs. George, Mrs. Rowlinson, and Mrs. F. R. Norman. The business meeting was after- wards held under the presidency of the Rev. T. Bracken- bury, the superintendent of the circuit. The financial statements which were presented by the stewards com- pared favourably with those for the corresponding period last year. The Chairman's numerical returns were also submitted and they showed a slight increase during the past three months. The Sunday school, day school:, and temperance schedules were else submitted. It was stated that that would be the last occasion on which the day school schedules would be produced as they had been transferred to the School Board, and Mr. John Simpson who had occupied the position as secretary and correspondent since they were opened over 40 years ago, made an interesting state- merit with reference to the cause which had led them to give up the management of the schools. It was decided that arrangements should be made for a tea meeting and reception in connection with the incoming of the new minister who is to succeed the Rev. W. Lila Stone. THE GENERAL ELECTION. Na official intimation has yet been given in the North- wich division of any candidate being put forward by the Conservative party to contest the seat in opposition to Sir John T. Brunner, Bart., M.P. Two gentlemen have been mentioned but nothing definite has been agreed upon. It will be remembered that Sir John Brunner's majority at the last election was 1,255 and this is thought by some to be formable enough to prevent a contest. He has fought the division four times and won thrice.

div.head: GALLANT RESCUE FROM DROWNING.
div.p: GALLANT RESCUE FROM DROWNING.

Whilst a number of youths were bathing in the Bridge- water Canal near Bates Bridge, Runcorn, on Tuesday, it was noticed that one of them hAd got beyond his depth and was sinking. Edward Field, of the Bird-in-Band public-house, immediately plunged iuto the water with- out divesting himself of his clothing, and succeeded in rescuing the unfortunate bather. This is not the first time Field has been instrumental in saving from drown- ing, and his conduct on this last occasion was most creditable to him. THE TECHNICAL INSTITUTE, RENCORNi

As will be seen from an announcement in another column, respecting the opening of the Runcorn Techni- cal Institute which is to take place on July 17th, it is urged that there be a ball-day holiday on that day, and that employers will be good enough to make such arrangements as to hours that their employe may not suffer any loss. The townspeople are asked to decorate the streets and ii.mses and to make the occmion worthy or the opening of an Institute which will play such an important part in the educational and industrial future of the town. The Technical Instruction Committee pro- pose to throw open the new Institute for the whole day for inspection. Music will be provided. It is expected that an appeal will be made to those who have curios and objects of interest to lend them for the occasion.

div.head: BUILDING ENOROACHNIENT AT FRODSLIAM.
div.p: A BUILDING ENOROACHNIENT AT FRODSLIAM.

At Frodsham Petty Sessions on Wednesday, the mag- istrates, Mr. C. Reynolds and Dr. Steele, were engaged for some considerable time in hearing a case in which Job William Rothwell, of Frodsham, was charged with unlawfully and without the consent in writing of tbe Runcorn Rural District Council, did build an addition to certain houses or buildings beyond the front ef other houses in Church-st., Frodsliam, on the 11th March,lB9s. Mr. Churton, solicitor, Chester, instructed by Mr. Linaker, solicitor, Frodsham, represented the defendant. Mr. Farrington, inspector of nuisances for the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, said he appeared there to prosecute, The action was takes under a section of the Public Health (Buildings and Streets) Act. It was taken in order to set at rest and prove whether there had been an encroachment over the building line which was ' granted by the Authority. Mr. Linaker on behalf el Mr. Rothwell submitted a plan for alteration of the premises in Church-street, Frodsham. Plans were deposited in the month of November, and he (dr. Far- rington) submitted them to the local parochial com- mittee. That authority declined to pass them on the grounds that the windows projected, too far into the street, and the matter was relegated to a committee for consideration. That committee met, and as a result of their recommendations on the 24th November, a resolu- tion was passed by the Parochial Committee that the projection could not be allowed. This was recorded on the minutes and adopted by the Rural District Council. Mr. Lioaker again submitted a plan which was refused by the committee, aid a resolution was passed that the building line be a straight line from the outside edge of an old bay window to the corner of the Golden Lion public-house.—Mr. Farrington was proceeding to give details as to the committee's action when Mr. Churton objected to them being beard, contending that they were unnecessary. He said the facts were simply these. The first plans submitted showed a prcrjection of 18 inches ; when the Council objected to it an amended plan showing one window to project 10 inches and the other 11 inches was submitted and approved of, and they had built their premises in accordance with the ap- proved plan.—Mr. Farrington, continuing, said the question the magistrates had to adjudicate upon was whether the buildings were in accordance with the amended plan. It would be a question of measure- ments between the two surveyors. In cross-examina- tion, witness said the width of the street in question from building 63 building was 49f I. 7in. at the southend and 42ft. lin, at the north end. On the amended plan one window was allowed to project 11 inches and another 10i inches. He admitted forwarding a letter stating that "the plans" had been approved by the committee.

Mr. William Owen, architect and surveyor, Warring- ton, said he was asked by Mr.Farrington to take certain dimensions in Church-street, Frodsham,and he did so on the 20th inst. The object of the dimensions was to show whether there had been an encroachment upon a building line when drawn from an old bay window to the outside corner of the Golden Lion. He found that One bay window encroached one inch and another two inches. 'The front window projected 11 inches at the South end, and 14 inches on the north end ; and the second window 12 inches on the south end and 113-8 on the north end. It was an encroachment beyond the resolution of the comtnittee. Mr. Churton for the defence said he thought that the magistrates would understand that those proceedings which he thought were moat vexatious and very un- necessary had been instituted by the casting vote of the Chairman of the meeting. It was quite clear that there was a very considerable difference of opinion as to whether it was right or just that the defendant should Spend a great deal of money in having to take down buildings which he (Mr. Churton) thought were an or- nament to the town,and which could not be said te be a nuisance. Their amended plans were passed, and he was prepared to stand or fall upon the letter received from Mr. Farrington, in which be stated that their plans had been approved. Mr. E. H. flamlyn, employed at Messrs. Linaker and Sons, said he drew up the plans for Mr. Rothwell's alter- tons in Church-st. He corroborated Mr. Churton's statement as to the projection allowed. His measure- ments were that the windows projected 14 inches in one case and 12i in another. The Magistrates retired to consider their verdict, and on their return Mr. Reyholds said they were satisfied that there bad been an encroachment because the evi- dence given by the last witness admitted it. They thought the best plan would be to adjourn the case to admit of the authority and Mr. Rothwell coming to 801110 agreement respecting the encroachment. Although the encroachment was very little,the case was very import- ant in principle. They would adjourn the case for a month.

div.head: WESTON POINT.
div.p: WESTON POINT.

SIIDDRN DIM= OF A CHILD. —On Saturday morning, about seven o'clock, Bertha Jinks, aged ten weeks, whose parents belong to Middlewich, but who live on a flat, was found dead in bed. The little one was appar- ently in go xi health when the father and mother retired with her on the fiat at Weston Point, at ten o'clock on Friday night, but on their awaking at seven o'clock next morning she was dead. The baby had enj,yed good health from birth.—Mr. J. E. Worslev conducted an in- quiry relative to the death of the child on Tuesday wowing. Alter evidence had been given by the parents and Dr. Bruntoo local tenens for Dr. McDougall, the jury returned a verdict of death from "Natural causes."

div.head: IiELSBY.
div.p: IiELSBY.

CHILDREN'S TBEAT.—The Sunday school scholars con- nected with Zion Cnaptd, Helsby, were provided with their annual treat on blouday afternoon. The scholars numbering about 100, together with between sixty and seventy triends,formed in procession and proceeded to a field kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. A. White. At the head of the procession there were the following offi- cials :—Messrs. B. Parker, John Noden, James Wurrall, Thomas Stagg, and John Williams. 'rue girls were in charge of the Messes Brandreth, Mrs. Noden' and Miss Alcock. An excellent tea was partaken of. Sports and various games were engaged in when prizes were com- peted tor. The weather was beautifully fine,aud a most enjoyable time was spent.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH Oi A RUNCORN LADY
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH Oi A RUNCORN LADY
AT SOUTHPORT.

On Wednesday morning Mrs. Robert Bennett,a widow formerly of Runcorn, and sister of Mr. Thomas Boote, Leinster Gardens, Runcorn, was found dead in a chair at her house in Gordon-street, Southport. The deceased lady was a native of Runcorn and had reached the ad- vanzed age of 70 years. Her husband died in Runcorn over 30 'ears ago. She had been living at Southport for a number of years and latterly had been in failing health, but would have no one in the house with her. On Tues- day, the neighbours noticed that she looked worse than usual ard not seeing her about on Wednesday morning, they broke open the door and found her sitting dead in her-chair with part of a loaf of bread in her lap. On the table by her side was a bread-knife, some tea in a cup, and also some sugar. A medical examination showed that she had died the previous night from an aortic affec- tion of the heart.

The Sheriff f Norwick on Thursday received a eome munication from Mr. Asquith intimating tMit the Queen had granted a respite in the case of Frank Mils, then lying in Norwich Gaol under sentence ot death for the murder of his wife. It is announced that Mr. D. A. Thomas, M.P., has secured from the Home Secretary a promise to provide for the appointment of practical colliers as;sub-assistant inspectors of mines.

pened a little oftener it would be better. It was not in his province to say that it was a danger to health.—Mr. Parr said there was a most serious smell at the new river diversion. It was something fearful and they could smell it half-way up Bridge-street, Warrington.—Mr. Farrington said the same remark applied to the old river by Wilderspool Causeway, and the river at Warrington Bridge. and also the Ship Canal. It was owing to the dryness of the weather and the low tides.—Admiral Jones Parry said he was afraid they could not do anything in the matter. Be did not think it would ever be possible to have clear water in the Ship Canal.—Dr. Adams Eaid little by little,Urban powers which drained their sewage into the canal and the river were being compelled to keep it out. It was the unwashed sewage which caused the smell. Re did not think they could do anything other than what was already being done by the Urban powers. Some recent Acts were being brought into force but it would be years and years before the Canal was arything like a purified waterway.— Admiral Perry said there would always be a , quantity of sewage from the vessels traversing the canal. —Dr. Adams said of course the ships contributed a cer- tain amount of sewage. That might be overcome by compelling them to keep it until they got into the open sea, as was the case with some canals an waterways. He understood that at present same 40 per cent. of Man- chester sewage was being kept out of tbe canal. There were so wiany vested interests and authoritie*mptying their sewage into it that it would take a long time be- fore they were stopped from doing so.—The Inspector stated that some of the sewers of their authority emp- tied into it. On the motion of Mr. Woodward, seconded by Mr. Heywood, it was decided that the matter be de- ferred until the modification of the boundaries,and that they join in any combined action to deal with the question.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

A meeting of this Board was held in the Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. J. Brandreth occupied the chair and there were also present in addition to the members of the Rural Council, Messrs. T. Hanley, J.P., S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., S."Yarwood, T. Lea, and Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), Mr. G. Ashtcn (deputy clerk) and Mr. Cunnah (workmaster).

div.head: ACCOMMODATION AT THE COUNTY ASYLUM.
div.p: THE ACCOMMODATION AT THE COUNTY ASYLUM.

Mr. Hamby, clerk of the County Asylum, Chester, wrote stating that notwithstanding the recent con- version of a dining room into a dormitory, there was but one vacant bed in the institution, and that recently the whole of the beds had been occupied, and cases re- fused admission. It was also stated that there were many chronic harmless cases in the asylum which might well be treated in the workhouse, and which if removed would make room for urgent and acute cases. He therefore irquired whether the Board had any accom- modation, or could provide accommodation in their workhouse for any such harmless cases in the Asylum belonging to the Runcorn Union, particularly females. —Mr.Flandley moved that the clerk write to the Asylum authorities stating that they had no accommodation at the house for such patients.—Mr. John Weir seconded the proposition, and it was carried. INCREASH OF A RELIEVINO OFFICTR'S SALARY.

Mr. Heywood stated that at a committee meeting with regard to Mr. Rile-'s applica- tion for lucre Ise of salary it was carried that the salary be increased to £lOO. The com- mittee were not quite unanimous on the matter, for out of a committee of seven there were two dissentients. He proposed that the report or the committee increasing the salary from £75 to £lOO be received and adopted.—Mr. Aaron seconded.—Mr. Parr wished to know upon what grounds Mr. Riley applied for an increase of salary.— Mr. Heywood read Mr. Riley's letter of application which has already been published.—Mr. Yarwood said he did not care to go in opposition to a committee, but he certainly must oppose the amount proposed to be given to Mr. Riley. He would have been willing to vote for an advance of £l5 but not £25. He proposed that Mr. Riley's salary be increased by, £ls.—Mr. T. Lea seconded.-11r. Parr did not think the present were times for raising salaries. It was cheaper to live now than ' when Mr. Riley was appointed. It was all very well for: people to be benevolent, but not with other people's money.—Mr. Wright said he knew Mr. Riley when he was on the Board previously, and he thought that his salary was a very small one. Since Mr. Riley was ap- pointed the rateable value of his district had increased 40 per cent. If they did not give good salaries they would not have the best men. He thougt.t that as the Bud. worth relieving officer had received the same advance,it would be a slur on Mr. Riley if they did not give him the advance.—Adiniral Jones Parry said there seemed to be a general opinion that the Budworth relieving officer was raised too much on the last occasion. It was a pity that these cases were not taken one with the other.—Mr. Williams said enough had been said to prove, not the benevolence, but the merits of the grant proposed by the committe. Those who had been accustomed to employ workmen for higher duties than farm labourers, could appreciate a good man, and he thought Mr. Riley should be rewarded accordingly after 20 years' service. He had art ived at a time in life when he had found It necessary to have a conveyance. By his close investigation into the cases he had had ta deal with, he had saved the ratepayers scores of pounds.—Mr. Mclntyre said his chief objection ta the increase was that it was one of 25 per cent. He thou7.ht that was rather too much and he should support the amendment. Mention had been made of the increase in Mr. De Pri--z's salary. That was given because there waS a pro4pectsve increase of three additional townships to his district. But there was no , such reasan for raising Mr. Riley's salary. He was an , efficient and conscientious officer but he thought the increase of £25 was too much.—Mr. Woodward said he should support the original propositien because he be- lieved Mr. Riley was badly paid. Mr. De Prez's salary was raised on his merits and in view of the possibility of the enlargement of his district there was a restriction made that he should not alt for an increase of salary when that took place.—Mr. Roylance said the chief ' reason given for the increase was that Mr. Riley was good at screwing poor people down to the lowest limit, (Cries of no, no).—lt was ultimately agreed by 12 votes to 8 to carry out the Committee's recommendation.

div.head: EITEN'SION OF THE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: THE EITEN'SION OF THE WORKHOUSE.

Mr. Handley propovd that the Guardians ask the con- sent of the Local Government Board to the extension of the Workhouse by building an additional ward on the male side of the house, over the pakum shop, for the accommodation of old men, not hoqpital patients, at a sum not exceeding £l5O. which should be borrowed to be repaid in 20 years.—Mr. Lea seconded the motion,and it was carried unanimously.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

Mr. Heywood submitted the report of the Financf Committee which showed that the expenditure was £477. The amount paid in ont•relief was about the same as usual. The balance at the hank was £3,43B.—Thereport was adopted.—lt was stated that the followinz town- ships had not paid their calls :—Alvanley, Bartington, Bud worth, Grappenhall, Hatton, and Halton (part) and Frodsham (part). It was decided that notices be sent to the overseers aqkine for payment. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

On Tuesday afternoon the fortnightly meeting of the above-named Council was held at Dutton Workhouse. Mr. J. Mclntyre, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were also present Admiral Parry, Messrs. J. Brandreth, H. E Heywood, W. M Williams, S. Woodward, J. Parr, J. S. Chadwick, T. Lewis, J. Weir, C. Roylance, E. Aaron, W. Pickering, W. Holt, G. Priestner, T. Darling- ton, and T. Wright ; Mr. Ashton (clerk), Mr. G. Ashton (deputy clerk), Mr. J. Farrington (nuisance inspector), Dr. Adams (medical officer), Mr. J. Swinton and Mr. W. Diggle (surveyors). WESTON WATER SUPPLY —TRH INSPECTOR'S REPORT. Writing on the 20th inst., Mr. Collier, clerk to the Weston Parish Council, stated that at a meeting of the Council on the 14th inst., the members had under con- sideration the report of a letter addressed by Mr. Mar- shall, secretary to the Runcorn Urban District Council, to the Rural District Council, on the water supply to Weston. He was instructed to call their attention to the fact that a large number of houses in Weston had not a sufficient water supply, some of the houses being whole days without any, which confirmed Mr. Aaron's statement on the point. His Council considered this a state of things that ought nit to exist, and hoped the matter would receive their due consideration with a view to an efficient supply of water being given to the township at the earliest possible moment.—Mr. Farring- ton on being asked to give his report concerning the water supply at Weston, said he visited Weston on the 17th inst.. and found that 13 houses situate between the "Round House" and the "Royal Oak Inn" in the male street had an intermittent supply. Seven others in the same line had a plentiful supply, and the cccupiers of fourteen houses also in the same lino had no complaints to make respecting the water supply. He found 45 houses entirely without a supply situated at the lower end of the main street near to and adjoining the Royal Oak. These houses were visited from 3.30 to 4.45 p.m. He also visited the house owned and occupied by Mr. Aaron, and although there was a one inch service pipe to supply this and the adjoining house there was no water not even through the stop tap fixed in the cell ir. It was possible that the intermittency might be caused by the service pipes from the mains being too few in Inumber and insufficient in calibre for the number of houses they were intended to supply, but he failed to see that this should be the cause of there being no water at all. He was informed that the main laid in the lower road was only three inches in diameter and it was possi- ble that the pipes might contain sostie corrosion and if so ithe flow of water would ha impeded and the capacity so much reduced as might reader it insufficient for the DUM ber of houses it was intended for. It would be ob- served from the foregoing that the statement read at the last meeting of the Council in reference to this matter was incorrect. In conclusion he might add that it was the duty of the Council to see that their district was pro- perly supplied with water.—Dr. Adams stated that at times there was scarcely any sepply at all. On ..me occasion when he tried a tap at Weston Point at a house where there had been fever it would have taken half-an- hour to fill a bucket —The Chairman said he would like to ask the Inspector how Weston was supplied with water when the undertaking was in private hands.—Mr. Farrington said there was then a better supply. —Mr. Aaron said when they had a complaint to make to the Water Works Company they were treated properly, hut now when they went to the Runcorn Council they could not get civility, and still they had to pay for water they never got. The consumption .of water was more under the old company than now,and yet the supply was now worse. From Thursday last week, until 2.30 on Saturday morn- ing, they were without a drop of water. The supply discontinued about six o'clock on Saturday night until Sunday morning. They had a nice supply that day,but on Monday and again when he came away that (Tues- day) morning they were without water. He could say this that if fever did break out at Weldon it would be very 'serious. He moved that the clerk write to the 'Secretary of the Urban Council enclosing the Inspector's report, and praying fcr a better water supply.—Mr. Brandreth seconded the motion.and it was carried unani- mously.

div.p: COUNCILLODS AND CARTAGN.

The Chairman in accordance with notice of motim, moved that the Clerk be authorised to apply to the justices for their license to empower any District Coun- cillor to contract for the supply or outage of materials within the parish he represents.--Mr. Wright seconded the motion, and it was carried. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr. Adams reported that at Halton measles hal broken out with epidemic force, chiefly in connection with school attendance, and the number of cases in- creased to such an extent that he recommended all the schools to be closed. The absentees from school were on 10th inst., 16 ; on the 17th, 60 ; and on the 18th, 70. The schools had been closed for a month. Three cases of scarlet fever had occurred at Appleton and four at Norlev. A case of diphtheria had occurred at Five Crosses, Frndsham, and at Hatton scarlet fever had broken out, chiefly amongst those attending the inrant school.—The report was adopted. This concluded the business.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

Palma COUNCIL MESTING.—A meeting of the Council was held in the Pctty Sessional Court House, Frodsham, on Friday evening. Mr. H. E. Heywood occupied the chair, and there were also present Messrs. J. M.Williams W. Shore, Peter Booth, W. D. Ringrose, J. Barrow, W. Youd, James Midge, Joseph Corker, T. Earlam, Mr. Dig,ele (surveyor), Mr. Farrington (inspector of nuis- ance), Mr. T. Rogers (engineer), and Mr. Ashton (clerk to the Runcorn Rural District Council). Mr. D. Thorne writing on behalf of the London and North-Western and Great Western Joint Railways, in acknowledgement of the Council's letter,stated that as he was at present ad- vised, no smell was being given fourth by the manure, except when it was being unloaded, and as they carried this traffic all over the country, the action of the Paro- chial Committee of the Frodsham Parish Council almost meant a prohibition of thoir doing so. He took it, how. ever, that this was not intended, and he should be glad to hear from them as to whether any suggestion was made for abating the noisance complained of. If so he Ahould be,glail to consider the matter and do all he could to meet the wishes of the committee. It was leSolved that Messrs. Williams, Shore, Rogers, and Youd be ap- pointed a committee t meet Mr. Thorne to discuss the matter, and that Mr. Thorne be ruidested to appoint an early day to meet the committee at Fred- sham station.—There was a discussion as to the advisability of instructing a solicitor to act on behalf of the council in the: proceedings insti- tuted against Mr. Rethwell, when it was ultimately resolved that it be referred to Mr. Shore,Mr. Farrington, and the Clerk of the Rural District Council to determine the matter and that they be authorised and empowered to instruct a solicitor accordingly.—An adjourned meet- ing of the Council was held on Monday evening, presided over by Mr. Heywood. There were also present: Messrs. J. M. Williams, Shore, Youd, Corker, Peter Booth,James Illidge, George Rodgers, John Barrow and Mr. Ashton (clerk). The Chairman of the Water Committee sub- mitted his report which was adopted. It was resolved , that proceedings be instituted by Mr. Farrington, the inspector of nuisances, against Robert Fletcher of Volun- teer-st., Frodsham, for supplying, and against Abraham Joynson, of the same strest for receiving water contrary to the provisions of the Water Works Clauses Act, 1847. It was also resolved that provided the trustees of the Free Church, Frodsham, have water laid on to the cot- tages adjoining the Free Church, water be supplied to the Free Church at the rate af 10s. per year.—lt was further resolved that the pumping station and machinery be insured against fire.

NEGLECT OF A CHILD. —Thomas Batters and Mary Butters, Volunteer•st.,were charged with cruelly illtreat- ing their child, John Butters aged 10 months,by neglect. ing same at Frodsham on the 25'h May.—P.C. Price stated that at 10.30 p.m., on the 23rd March, from in- formation received he went to the residence of the two defendants. He saw that both of them were drunk. Be took the youngeSt child to Dr. Selby and he examined it. He informed witness that the child bad been neg lected, and he cautioned the female defendant. On the 25th Maw he saw the defendant going home drunk at midnight, and be told her he should report her. He again went down to the house on the 17th of the pre• sent month and found the child in the cradle, crying. There was no one in the house. He examined the child and bed, and found it in a very wet condition. He could not find the female defendant anywhere. She re- turned home drunk at eleven o'clock at night.—Dr. Selby. Frodsham, said the child was fully developed, and up to the average size at birth. A few months after the birth he was called to the house of the defendants. As no one answered the doer he walked in and found the child crying, with- out anyone in attendance. The child looked extremely and required food. On the third occasion when he visited the child it was from instructions from the police. It was then looking better. But there was want of substance about the legs. arms, and face, and Its weight was only 13Ibs. 12 instead of it being about 20Ibs. He was of the cpinion that up to a few weeks ago the child had not had good food. It had been better looked after since proceedings had been instituted and the child was now gaining weight. —Evidence was given by Phaehe Worrall, Esther Brett, Elizabeth Perci- val and Elizabeth Davies who proved that the female defendant was often drunk and repeatedlv neglected the child by leaving it alone in the house.—The Chairman said they had decided to let the male defendant off with a reprimand but his wife would be fined 40s. and the costs £2 75., or in detault one month's hard labour. Drumm AND DISORDERLY.—John Pemberton for bsing drunk and disorderly in Chester Main-road, Frcittham, On the 28th May was fined 5. and costs. A CYCLIST FINED.—CIPITIeS Owen GASSett was sum- moned for riding a bicycle without having a lighted Imp in Chester Main-road at flelsby on the 27th May. Be was fined 2s. 61 and costs.

ORHAT SANHBY SCHOOL BOARD—The monthly meet- ing of the above Board was held on Tuesday afternoon in the Rlard room at the schools, Great Sankey. Mr. W. P. Skelton presided, and there were also present the Rev.E.Sandys Jackson,Mr. Henry Bate. Mr. W. D. Jeans, I jun., (clerk) awd Mr. George Clarke (headmaster).—The :;lerk repotted that there was a balance in hand in favour of the Board of £35 151. 2d.—Mr.Clarke reported that the average attendances during the past three weeks had been 293.8, 307 and 299.5 respectively.—A suggestion was made to alter the hour of meeting to suit the convenience of one or two of the members. A short discussion took place, but no alteration was made, and the meeting will, therefore, be held as usual, namely. at 2 30 p tn. on the last Tuesday in each month.—The Rev. E. S. Jackson tendered his resignation of the office of vicc-chairman of the Board on the ground of his in- ability to regularly attend the meeting. He pointed out that he was elected to the positson during his ab- sence.—The resignation was then accepted, and it was understood that Mr. Jackson's successor would be ap- pointed at the next meeting...—This was all the business.

div.head: THUNDERSTORM.
div.p: THE THUNDERSTORM.

The Thunderstorm on W(dnooday was felt over a very wide area. In the showyard of the It.iyal Agricultural Society at Darlington rain began to tall heavily a few minutes after the Duke and Duchess of York had. left. It was accompanied by vivid lightning and heavy peals of thunder. Five visitors who were sheltering under a large tree in the centre of the ground were struck, and two of them—Mr. William %%storm, timber merchant, West Hartlepool, and Mr. T. T. Mawaton, farmer,Fence Houses, Durham—afterwards succumbed to their in- juries. Two miners were killed at Normanton while re- turning from work. Extensive damage was caused at Sheffield and at Malpas,Cl-,eshire, by flooding. In Man- chester some damage was done by the enormous rainfall. A number of men working in a sewer in Harpurhey had a narrow escape from being swept away. One of them was severely hurt.

Mr. M. Arrandale (Labou—r and Liberal candidate) was on Monday elected to the Manchester City Council to fill a vacancy caused by the elevation of Mr. Ashcroft (Con- servative) to the office of alderman. His opponent was Mr. A. Fulton (Conservative). The votes were : Arrandale, 854; Fulton, 746.

PRESENTATION OF A MEDAL.

At a special meting held in the Y.M.C.A. Hall, Mount Pleasant, Liverpool, on Saturday evening, an ambulance demonstration was eiven by members of number one division, central district. St. John Ambulance Associa- tion. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Hope Simpson, who was supported by Mr. W. Adamson (chairman Southern Hospital), Dr. Jones, Dr. L. Morgan. and the Rev. V. H. C. Moyle, of the Runcorn clergy staff. There was a large atteadance. An interesting feature of the proceedings was the presentation by the chairman of a special medal, and a diploma to Mr. William Hughes, Of 31, Princess-street, Runcorn, for an act of bravery In saving the lives of his fellow workmen at the risk ..of his own life. It a pp-s red that some time ago Hu.2hes was following his etnr.:ovinent at the Ferry Hut, Runcorn, when he saw som •in ht wagons, released by the break- ing of a coupline, running down an incline towards a cutting in whiol, alinut 40 men were working. He rp 9 to the points hill was, down the inclini oLnd was ji.i• • time to throw the runaway waggons off the line. heroic act, which saved the lives of the men below. fortunately cost Mr. Hughes both his 12,ZP. Having L. first treated at Latchford, he was brought to the Liv-r- -pool Southern Hospital. The medal bare the following inscription : " Awarded by the Grand Priory of the Order of the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem in Eng- land. For service in the cmilie of humanity. Presented to William Hughes, June, 1895."

Mr. W. Adainson., at thc;-riTquest of the Chairman, gave a detaile tirrount of the accident, and stated the- difficulty they experienced in obtaining the real facts of the case from Mr. Hughes. When these were ascertained they found no difficulty in getting a suitable recognition, from the highest autliority, of the heroic deeds per- formed. (Anplailite.)
The Chairman, having referred to Mr.Ffußbes'hernic act, said he had great pleasure in presenting the medal to Mr. liughes.

lir. Hughes wa; then assisted to the platform amid the applause of the company, which was continued until the ceremonial of oreßentation had been performed. • Mr. Hughes then asked that Mr. David Smith of Run- corn, the local stcretary of the C.E.U., might reply ca his behalf.

Mr. Smi•.ll necordingly conveyed to those present the heartfelt gratitude of Mr. and Mrs. Hughes for the kind way in which they had been received that evening. There could be doubt that the ceremony was a brotherly recounition of a genuinely heroic deed—such an act as not only the doctors. surgeons, and nurses of the Royal southern Hospital of Liverpool were proud to acknowifdgo, hot all thote who were engaged in public vp,pits throughow tie country. Applause.) Then f 41.0. red a displav or ambulance work, under the dint-lion of nr. Li.ellyn Morgan. Furtious DRIVING.—DanieI Basnett, Preston-o'th-Hill, was charged with driving a horse and cart furiously in Horssmarket-5t., on the 9th June.—Sergeant Cheney and P.C. Turner, gave evidence which showed that de- fendant was travelling at about 10 or 11 miles an hour, ' and that he disregarded their attempts to stop him.— He was fined 10s. and costs (21 58. 61.) MISCHIEVOUS YOUNGSTERS. —Clement Waddington (11), 18, St. James's-St.; samuel Campbell (7), 7, Bakehouse- yard, and John Burke (7), same address were charged with thro-ving missiles to the danger of passengers, in the public street.—P.C. Sankey said he saw the defen- dants throw a piece of wet horse-dung at a lady passing in a 'bus, the filth striking her in the eye. The Magis- trates ordered Burke and Campbell to receive three strokes of the birch, and Waddington, who did not ap- pear, six st 4tes. OBSTRUCTiON.—DEAVY PENALTY.—John Bartley, 4, Stanley-St., John Griffin, Peter Skully, William Coyne, Patrick Dooney, Thomas Lomax, and Joseph Leonardy, all of 'I urner-st., were charged with obstructing the pas- sage of Winwick-St., and refusing to move when re- quired. Bartley was the only one who appeared, and pleading guilty, was fined 58. a ndlcosts or 14 days in gaol. The other youths were, on the evidence of P.O. Clough, each fined 40s. and costa or one month hard labour in default. TUEsDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman), Dr. T. S. Smith, and Councillor a Roberts. Danwirenness.—Patrick Reardon was fined Sc. and costs for being drunk and disorderly on Pinner's Brow, on the 13th June. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr, John Fairclough (chairman) Messrs. G Geddes and J. H. Fleming. ARRESTED ON THE DOWNWARD PATH.—MarRaTeL Han- kinson, 17, was charged with stealing from 17 Carlisle street, between the 24th and 25th inst a saucepan and child's frock value Is. the property of Henry Fisher; she was also charged with stealin., from 13 Carlisle-street a woman's bodice the property or Hannah Varley.--Detec- tive Sergeant Monaghan said that this girl and another had been sle.eping out in the neig,hbourhood of the thefts for a number of nights and on Tuesday the property was missed and reported to witness who found the prisoner in the streets. She was taken to the Police Station and there confessed to having taken the articles and sold them at Chorley's marine stores. The prisoner and the other girl who was in court, were on their parents' permission hand,!..l over to Mr. H. Taylor, P.C.M. who pr3mised to get them installed into a home,—A convic- tion was recorded against Hankies m, the bench remark- ing that it was lucky they were arrested as it was evid- ent they were on the road to ruin. THURSDAY. —Before the Mayor ,(chairman), land Alder-

man Sutton. NISINTENANCE ORDER.—Robert Charles Worrall, Earlestown was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to contribute to his father's maintenance in the Warrington Union. —Mr. Shearer represented the Guardians, and said that defend- ant was able to pay 43. a week.—An order was made for this amount and costs. CRUELTY TO ANIMALS.—James Warburton, 35 Scott- at., was charged with having illtreated a horse by work- ing it while in an unfit state on the 17th June; John Barton, Birchall-Bt., was charged with causing it to be worked.—lnspector Luff said the animal on the day in question was at work lame. It was suffering from side- bone and ring-bone, and was only fit to work on sott land.—On defendant Barton promising to sell the animal for this purpos9 the case was dismissed on payment of ccsts.—William GrCellW3y, 22 Erwood-et., was charged with committing a similar offence on the lfich June.— Inspector Luff proved that the animal was totally unfit for work.—Defendant's plea of ignorance, and that the ' animal had been since destroyed was accepted, and he was dismissed on payment of costs.

DARESBURI rEt Y SESSIONS. TVESDA.Y.—Before &Ir. H. Nield (chairman), and Mr. Fl. Talbot. FURIOUS Dravtxo.—William Norman and George Shaw were each charged with furiously drivin7 a horse and cart along Chester-road, Thelwall, on June 7th. P.C. Robinson proved the case. It was stated by Shaw that his horse was restive, and he pulled it up a. soon as he collie. Each defendant was fined 53. including costs.— Thomas Ellison and John Basnett were also fined in a similar amount for furiously driving a horse and cart in Moore, on June llth.—P.C. Robinson also proved

this case. ILL-TREATING A CANAL HORSl3.—Thonlas Rieby, a boy employed as driver of a canal horse, was charged with ill-treating a horse at Stockton Heath, on May 29th, and Henry Rigby was charged with causing it to be ill- treated.—Mr. Holland, of Stockton Heath, said that he . saw the defendant with the horse on the above date on the canal bank at Stockton Heath. The horse was lying down, and appeared to be in a very exhausted state.— Mr. Sharrocks stated that he went to the boy who was crying bitterly. He said that the horse could not get along. Witness with some others had great difficulty in gettieg the horse on to its legs, and when it was got into a standing position it cou,d scarcely walk,as it was only" skin and bone." The boy told witness that the horse had come from Manchester to Runcorn and evaS then returning to Manchester, aed it had only two hours rest at Runcorn. Witness would have lodged the horse in his own stable, but the boy refused to allow him to do so. He afterwards lashed the horse, and then witness reverted the matter to Sergeant Gosling, who sent P.C. Brew and he horse was taken into the stable at London Bridge.— P.C. Brew said that the horse had pilled a II t from Manchester to Runcorn, a distance ef 33 miles, and it ! had then got back to Stockton Heath, with scarcely any rest or refreshment. When examined in the-stable, it had a raw wound under thi. collar. Henry Rigby was seen the next day, and he admi,ted sending the horse out.—lnspector Leff, R S.P.C.A., said that the horse was an old one, and very emaciated. It was totally unfit to do the work it had done.—The Bench inflicted a penalty of 103. arid costs upon Henry Rigbe, and fined Thomas Rigby the costs. INFRINGEMENT OF THE WEIGTITS AND MEASURES ACT,— Frederick W. H dlivood was cbarged with having a two lb. weight which was unjust, in his possession at Pres- ton Brook, on June 19, and also with having in his possession a pair of scales which were not stamped as revired by the Weights and Measures Act —Mr. Liird. the inspector of weights and measures for the county of ;Chester, proved the case:—A representative of Mr. Hall- wood said that he was not aware that the weight was , under weight, The Beneh inflicted a peealty of £1 and costs in each ca:e.—Alfred Dalin, tanner, was charged with having in his posseisien at Grappenhall, on June 13, four 56 lb.weights which were unjust,and also a pair of scales which were unjaet.—Mr. Hallerd,the inspector for the district proved the case.—Mr. Dakin said that he was not aware that the scales and weights were unjust. He also said that they were simply used to check the contractors bundles of leather, and were not used for selling. It was however ruled in a recent cac that the Weights and Measures Act applied to this case, in accordance with a test cane which had been recently heard, and the Bench inflicted. a penalty of is. and Costs in each case. DRUNICENNESS.—Anthony Daley, was fined si. includ- ing costs for being drunk and disorderly at Grapp,nhall on June 16th. P C. Milliugton proved the efts,. .jIefIiWZZLED Doos —Will;am Wakefield, Appleton, was fined with costs, and John Pemberton, Appleton, ss. and costs for allowing their dogs to be at large ere muzzled. A LOVER OF PANSIES.—Arthur Belfield, was charged with doing damage to fiewers to the extent of is., the property of Sir Gilbert Greenall, on June 11th. Mr. Fowler, who represented Sir iiilbeet Greenall, stated that Pee,. Gosling saw the defendant coming from the footpath of a house in Walton, and upon seeing him the defendant ran away, P.S. Gosling followed him and caught him, but upon searching him he found nothing. On walking a little way along the canal, however, he found a nutnner of pansies. P.S. Gosling corroborated Mr. Fowler's statement, and defendant was fined 10s. and costs. RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Beforo Mr. James Handley (chairman),Mr. 1. Rigby, and Mr. S. Taylor. THE ABATEMFNT OF A NOISANCE.—Thomas Henry Carr, jeweller, Runcorn, was summoned for neglecting to carry out an order for the abatement of a nuisance at 31, and 33, 13ridgewater-street. and 52, and 54, Reeent. street, issued by Mr. James Percival on behalf of the Runcorn Urban Council.—Mr. F. A. Lake, law-cler to the Council, prosecuted, and handed to the magietrates a plan of the houses. Be said the nuisance arose threugh the unsatisfactory position of the privies and eshpite. In two of the houses the privies actually adjoined the kitchen wall and the entrance to them was close to the living room. In the two other houses the privy was two feet in One case and two feet nine inches in another from the kitchen. The a.shnite were uncovered and were in a wet condition. There had been sickness in the houses for some years. The paving of the yarda was also very unsatisfactory. The order asked for the privies to be removed and that each house be provided with a water close, and ash box,and also that the yards he paved with something having a smooth surface.— Mt... James Percival proved serving the defendant with an order for the abatement of the nuisance on the 4th. April. There were measles in the houses at the present time. Nothing had been done to abate the nuisance.— The defendant admitted that a nuisance existed but said the authorities were the creators of it. The privies were put in their present position some years ago by the order of the Surveyor. They were then in the centre of the yard, and he thought it was a hardship upon him to be obliged to keep removing them. HA complained that the Urban Council had not proceeded under the 38th section of the Public Health Act.—Mr. Lake stated that if they had taken proceedings under that section of the Act it would have been more expensive for the defendant as the Authority would have done the work and made him liable for all expense. The Urban Council had been very lenient with him.—ln answer to the Chairman as to whether he therieht the rerriremente were reasonable. the defendant said he thought they were reasonable,and they would have been done months ago if he had had the means to do them.—The Chairman asked whether the houses were not occupied.—The defendant admitted that they were, but said he received very little rent.— The Chairman said the Council had power to close them. fun defendant said there were several nuisances being abated by the Urban Council for people in the town,town councillors included, and he did not see why he should not be treated the same. He had not the means to do it himself or he would have done.—Mr. Lake said if it was a question of the defendant wanting the Authority to do ' do it they would do so, but it would be more expen,ive for him. It was merely a question of the health of the residents with the Authority.-1 he Chairman said the magistrates thought the requirements of the Authority were reasomable, and they hoped the detendant would carry out the terms of the order as speedily as possible. They would make an order that the whole be completed by the 25th September. THEFT OF A GLASS.—Martha Perry,a married woman, of Weston Point, was charged with having on Saturday stolen a half-pint glass the property of Susan Fitton.—A girl, eight years of age,named Jane Andrews stated that on Saturday afternoon about 2 30. she was washing some glass in the bar at the Watermen's Arms, Weston Point, when she saw the prisoner take the glass from the coun- ter, put it in her pocket and go away with it.—Mrs. Fitton said she asked prisoner whether she had taken a glass, but she denied doing HO. Witness then took the glass from the prisoner's pocket.—Prisoner stated that she did not know it was in her pocket.—The magistrates committed her to prison for seven days. AN OLD OrFENDEß.—Elizabeth Barker, who has ap- peared before the Bench intermittently for a period of ten years, was charged with lodging in an unoccupied house in Back Cooper-st., on the 2rrd inst ,without hav- ing any visible means of subsistence.—P.C. Gregory stated that at one a.m. on Sunday he saw the prisoner with a man sleeping in an unoccupied house in the street mentioned.—She was sent to gaol for seven days. A BATCH OF BEGGARS. Samuel Tennant, John Lord, and James Smith, who stated that they belonged to Blackburn, were charged with beg- ging in High-street, Runcorn, on Saturday. The prisoners stated that drink was given them by an old " mate." They came over here thinking they could find a job at haymaking. The Superintendent jocularly remarked that there was no haymaking in the middle of a town.—The magistrates committed the pri- sonen to Knutsford prison for seven days.—James Hardy fora like offence was similarly dealt with. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Rese Ann Corcoran was r charged with being drunk and disorderly in Mersey-at. on the 23rd inst.—P.S. Lee proved the case.—Ori promising to give up taking the drink she was dis- charged. Th.:MUZZLED DOGS.—The following were fined for allow- ing their dogs to be at large unmuzzled :—William Sheen 7, Porter-st. ; John Talbot, Whitechapel-St., Weston Point ; Henry Smetham, 30, Egerton-st.. Runcorn. SCHOOL ATTENDANCES CASES.—JOhni Gratton, Wick- stone hill, Runcorn ; and Peter Stubbs, Stone-st., were each fined 6d. and 4s. 6d. costs for neglecting to cause their children to attend school regularly. Mr. Thomas Bowyer prosecuted.
