div.head: LONGFELLOW'S LONGING.
div.p: LONGFELLOW'S LONGING.

" Oh I world, so few the years we lire, Would that tla life which thou dost give Were life indeed t" In the Poets' Corner, Westminster Abbey, is a beautiful tablet to the memory of the American poet who wrote these lines—Henry W. Longfellow—erected by his English friends and admirers. Upon the whole his splendid verse expressed the sombre side of life. And yet is not that the more conspicuous side? To say truth, it is. For this there are many reasons, chief among which is, no doubt, bodily pain and ill-health. " I lost all the pleasures' of life," writes a lady. Then she tells us why. "For over twenty years," she says, " I suffered more or less from indigestion. In the early part ot 1888 I began to feel the complaint more acutely. I was always tired, languid, and weary ; everything seemed a trouble to me. My skin was sallow, and the whites of my eyes tinged yellow. I had a constant feel- ing of sickness and inclination to retch. My mouth tasted badly, my appetite failed ; in fact when food was placed before me I could scarcely touch it. And after what little I did eat I was seized with great pain at the chest and sides. I suffered severely from wind, fre- quently belching it up. After a time I began to lose my steep, and night after night I would lie awake. " I got very week, thin, and emaciated, and so low. spirited that I lost all the pleasures of life. For week together I felt too weak to leave the house and had no desire for company. %herever I went I felt languid, tired, and worn out, and was never free from pain. I consulted doctor after doctor, who gave me medicines, but I grew no better. The doctors said I had got con. gestion of the liver, and I took various kinds of liver medicines, but all to no purpose. I also tried change of air, but found no benefit from it, and continued to exist in this miserable way year after year. " In October, 1892, a friend of mine, Mr. Bruce, of Liverpool, tole. me of the remaikable benefit his niece had derived from a medicine called Mother Seigel's Cura tive Syrup. And this, after several doctors, including_ a specialist, bad failed to do her good. Although I had no faith that anything would help me, I commenced taking this preparation, and in a few days I found that my sickness was less and I could digest my food better. I gradually became stronger and stronger, and I now feet better than I have done for twenty years. "I have told many of my friends of the marvellou s benefit I have derived from Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and if you think tit to publish this statement you can do so. (Signed) (Mrs.) Lonsta A. E. Cox, The Woodlands, Somerville, Seacombe, December, 20th 1892," Speaking of an exceedingly happy episode of his life, the great Anglo• American orator, Mr. John B. Gough, uAed to say, " It was one of the days of God, which are a thousand years." Life is not mere length, but depth and breadth. When in health we distil enjoy- ment from almost everything ; when ill, trifles are burdensome, the heat is gone from the sunshine, and we walk in self-created shadows. What Mother Seigel did for our correipondent she has done, and is daily doing, for multitudes of her suffering sisters in all lands. What mission can be more praise- worthy and mere productive of solid good? She helps us to realise "life indeed."

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY.-TIIE RESIGNATION OF TEIE GOVERN-
mENT.

When the House of Commons assembled on Monday aftrnoo.n Sir WILLIAM liesconwr made a statement on the Ministerial situatien, tie said the divisim on the previous Friday nieht on the vote for the War Office was in fact a direct vote of censure on the Secretary for War, and the Gwerninent absolutely identified thetnelves with his right hon. friend and his army administration. The course taken by responsible gentlemen opposite had disabled the WAR SECRETARY from proceeding with the . Army Estimates, and had made it practically impossitle ' for the Executive Government to obtain those votes which were necessary for the public service. The Cabinet had therefore found it their duty to tender to the QUEEN their resignation of office, and that resigna.- tion had been accepted. The Government accordingly only held cffice till their successors were appointed. At four o'clock, en the motisin of Mr. ASQUITH, the Howe adjourned. -

Lord RCV,ERERY, in informing the Houso of Lords that the Goveroinent had resigned, said that afte r the vote of the House of Commons on Friday night, which was nracticady a vote of censure OR the SECRETARY of STATE for WAR and the department over which lw presided,on quEstion of national defence, immediately after he had adumbrated to the House a great scheme of military re- organisatioh, the Government felt it to he their duty to place their resignations in the hands of FIER MAJESTY. Those resignations had been accepted, and consequently they only held office until their successors had been ap- pointed.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT THE VULCAN FOUNDRY.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT THE VULCAN FOUNDRY.

Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at the Police Station, Warrington, lon Monday, on the borly of William Sud- ger who was fatally injured at the 'Vulcan Foundry and died at the Warrington Infirmary on Saturday after- noon.—Mr. Brighouse said that the inquiry was as to the death of the deceased who was engaged at the Vul- can Foundry by Messrs. Booth, for the purpose of put- ting up a crane—Mr. Rowland Tinker, H.M. Inspector of Factories ot Moses (Sate, Bolton, and Mr. Norman on behalf of the Vulcan Foundry were present,. Mr. Booth was also present. Francis James Maud said that the deceased was his son-in-law, and resided at Airedale View, Rodlev, Leeds. He was 28 years of age, and was employed by Messrs. Booth Bros., Rodlev, steam crane works. Witness saw him alive about a week previous when he was going to the Vulcan. He was then in good health. Reuben Tomkinson said that he was in the employ of the Vulcan Company, and was working under the direc- tion of the deceased. They were engaged ia " squaring " the crane, when the deceased fell down to the floor. Witness could not explain what caused his fall. He was as to once taken out of the works. Joseph Naylor gave similar evidence. Nurse Rill, of the Warrington Infirmary,gave evidence of the death of the deceased. Inspector Tinker, who produced photographs of the scene of the accident, said that he had no fault to find with the state of the machinery at the place where the man fell. It was impossible to take steps to prevent it. It was his opinion that the deceased was pulling at a lever, and the lever must have slipped, and thus thrown him to the ground. Mr. Booth said that the deceased was a life long teeto- taler and was an excellent workman. The jury returned a vet diet of "Accidental Death."

div.head: PREDICAMENT.
div.p: A PREDICAMENT.

Soon after the outbreak of the Cuban insurrection an American newspaper determined to send a special cor- respondent to the seat of war. The journal in question had been getting some smart reports from its regular correspondent at a point in Florida, and the special cor- respondent was ordered to stop at this point and take the Floridian to Cuba with him. In a day or two the telegraph editor received the following message from the special : "Or correspondent here seems very much disinclined to go to Cuba with me." The editor was determined not to have his plans balked, and sent this: —" Our Florida cerrespondent must obey orders and go to Cuba with you. Offer any reasonable inducements." Not long afterwards the following reply was received "Our correspondent refuses point blank to go to Cuba wish me except upon one condition, and that is that I marry her. I have one wife already, and I am afraid the war will be over before I can get a divorce. Answer quick."

div.head: tetterfs to the etittor.
div.p: tetterfs to the etittor.
WARRINGTON CORPORATION AND THE STATE
OF THE RIVER.

The first duty of a Corporation is to guard the health of the inhabitants under its control. It seems to me that the Council of Warrington consider that the health of the town is of minor importance to that of the rates. At all events they do not appear to be moving with the question of the pollution ot the river. At present the condition of the river in and about Wilderspool is very little better than that of a " cesspool." I wonder if it occurs to any of our town councillors that as the tide rises they get back part of the refuse into the sewers again. Warrington may be visited by epidemics from time to time but no real effort is made to grapple with the causes. As the river is at present, instead of being a sovirce of health to the inhabitants of the town it is a source of danger, and the smells whish emanate there- from are a disgrace to the intelligence of our town coon- CiHors. When are they going to do their duty with this grave question ?—Yours &c., E. E. ,

div.head: LIBERAL POLITICS.
div.p: LIBERAL POLITICS.

See,edtbere iSLO subject which commands a larger amount of general and legitimate public interest than the evolution of modern democracies. That is what gives • deeper significance and importanee to our party war- fare. For politica reflect this evolution, and, therefore, • survey, or rather a partial survey of the present poli- tical position, may not be out of place; at any rate, it is just as well for Liberals to take stock at a time, when, with a general election imminent political meteorolog- ists tell us our immediate prospects in the country are— well, not just as rosy as they might he. If I might venture to express an opinion to those of the same way of thinking, I should say in the first place that no temporary party defeat, or the probability of it, should make us despond. Because in reality, and in respect of the principles we have been fighting for all along, we have not beaten at all. Our record is one long list of victories continued up to the present time— not omitting the excellent work of the present Govern- ment—and our opponents may thank their stars that Liberal policy has established the healthiest, soundest, and most enduring form of Conservatism in our great democracy. Such being our record, what, apart from the usual swine-swang of English politics, are the causes which seem likely to bring about a transference of political power at the next election ? What are some of the forces which, just now, appear to be drivicg, or attract- ing the political tide towards the shores of Conservatism. 111 the first place, we know that after a period of sus- tained political tension, the country, generally speaking, is inclined to take it easy for a time. With your per- mission,l will give one homely illustration of this. I was talking the other day to a farmer in Worcestershire about the question of the House of Lords acd the House of Commons. " Well," he said, "I think we have had enough of both of them. I would clear them out for five years, and lock the place up. I would'nt pull it down. They might keep it aired "—this was a most practical man—" and cleaned, but I'd serve them same as old Oliver did." Apparently our bucolic friend would have the House (as it is called like other Workhouses) not only cleaned, but purged and possibly whitewashed into the bargain ! Allowing for the exaggeration we are accustomed to, in reflections, I think this view of things corresponds to a prevalent frame of mind. And it is rather a poser for reformers. But what will be the effect on the mind of a man like this, of such revolutionary proposals as we have recently heard of from Norwich and Newcastle ? The official attitude of the Liberal Press to these proposals, is not unnaturally one of smiling in- difference, but there is a serious side to them as well, for these communistic vapourings mean dropping the bone for the shadow with a vengeance. No doubt they are well meant. We know there are plenty of sincere and unselfi.h socialists. But that is no excuse for indulging in vague illusions, which people do not trouble to sift to the bottom, and indulgine in them at the expense of what is practical and feasible ; more especially as 1 those who persist in doing so, injure others as well as themselves. I will not occupy your space by go- ing over old ground in discussing Socialism. In the sense of what is subversive and destructive of individual- ism and intended to put an end to competition, we all know it is impossible. And if it were possible, and the experiment could be tried in this country ; if we got rid of combativeness of English character, and turned ourselves into a race of State-regulated machines under the heel universal officialdom, what would be our national position ? Do ideal Socialists ever put the seuestion ? They seem utterly oblivious, or careless, of the fact that we should stand to be crushed politically and commercially by our ambiticus rivals abroad. It is -simply ridiculous to talk about abolishing individualism, and the mere effect to undermine it is destructive of those very altrustic sentiments which are the hope of our future civilisation. The two elements of altruism and individualism must continue and develop along side of each other, and our business has been to regu- late and adjust that growth in so far as it is safe or wise for Government to interfere at all. The greater part of what is termed heroic legislation having been completed during a century of Liberal effort, our duties must be- come more and more a matter of good administration. The present Government, thanks in a large measure to Mr. Marley and Mr. Asquith, shines in administratinn.le legislation, it has done work of vital importance, but events have made it impessible for them to proceed with further urgent measure? of reform. The question ia.how long the country will have to go without them. When shall we be able, so to speak, to put in the key stone and the coping stones to the Liberal arih. We may be very sure of one thing, that the less support the mem- bers of the IL.?. receive, the sooner this work will be done. The proposals of this party, decent Englishmen, as the " Spectator "observes, whether they be peers or platelayers, will not stand. The " Spectator " recently had an important article on this sutdect. Our old friend is, a little grandmotherly .and goody-goody, but now and again it comes out forcibly, as for instance, in this article which appeared in the issue for April 20 h, of -which I give tht following extract :—" The Indepen- ! dent Labour Party does not affront and alarm capital- ! ists alone, or capitalists and the cultivated classes, but it terrifies and ogends also, all who hope for property, all who believe in thrift as an instrument for securing comfort, and the whole body of workmen who have either fairly paid work, or who have confidence in them- selves and their faculties, that is, probably four fifths, certainly three fifths of the whole community. Those will all recoil before such a programme as this, and most of them will feel, unfair as the feeling may be, that if this is the result to which Ridicalisin or Liberalism. tinged with Socialism tends, then they must cease to be either Radicals or Liberals, and consent however re- luctantly, to allow " reactionaries "to accede to power. , Every blow by Anarchists makes scores of thousands of Conservatives, and resolutions such as those of the to- dependent La.:lour Party, though they do not shock the moral sense of the community,like the crimes of Anarch- ists, do shock almost in an equal degree the intellectual sense Mr. Kier Herdie is at this moment a more dangerous foe to the Liberal or R tdicel Party than Mr. Balfour or any other leader of the Opposition." Now there is a good deal of truth in this; hut we may note in passing, that Liberalism does not tend to Social- ism. If we compare for a moment our position with that of our neighbours—and cousins—we shall find plain proof of that. Lot us take Germany and America for Instance. In Germany tho drift of the Government for about a generation, was alinittedly anti-liberal, and very possibly a strong autneratic Government was ex- actly what the country required for the time. Rut as a result of this and especiallse perhaps, as a result of the , attempt to contione the same regime beyond the time that called for it, there has sprung up a body of Social- ists more numerous than any other single party in the Empire. In the States of America, we see a different State of things. Less individual liberty than in this country, but still, in their great eommercial world, in- dividualism run mad. and a c-ntrast betwean the extremes of wealth and poverty, far vv,,rse than what it is in this country. This tends to spread, not Conserva- tism, but unrest and hatred between class and class. They said we were doing so during the years when Rus- sel, Peel, Cebdee, Bright, and Gladstone were carrying !their great measures of political emancipation. On the contrary. we were creating the Conservatism of to-day, a Conservatism which we have increased by subse- quently carrying those constructive measures by which we have helped to modify and temper, and, as it were, soften down the results or individualism. And to-day you hay,- a stronger Conservative bias, therefore, run- ning through democracies that have been governed on the lines of Switzerland and England. than. taking them AS a whole, you End either in G,,rmany or the States. -Our opponents have really a great deal to th k ua for,

but gratitude in these matters, is not their strong point, and it's precious little thanks we do get from them for our pains. So much for the arguments and insinuations often made that we are responsible for the wild doctrines preached in certain quarters. We are not responsible. On the contrary, it is we who have made their authors impotent for evil, and destitute of influence with the mass of the nation. hut we have to pay the penalty all the same.

When Karl Marx's revolutionary emissaries went into Switzerland, they very quickly turned the country Con- servative, and so it has bees here. For the ordinary voter declining to go into the niceties of the situation, and scared by these chimeras, bluntly says that if this is what comes of making changes, he will have no changes .

Thre'n I think we are suffering from the position taken up by some sections of Trade Unionists. Liberalism is no enemy to Trade Unions. We are blind neither to the necessity there has been for them, nor to the benefit they have conferred. Collective bargaining Ms been and is still necessary, and the working class of the kingdom are entitled to the !argent share of such mutual advantage as English manufacturers may have in one way or an- other over Continental competitors. But when skilled labour of any kind lays it down that they will only work on terms which make it impossible for manufacturers to continue except at a loss, and when, in consequence, we see plant thrown idle, trade diminished, and the ranks of the unemployed swelled, well, to put it mildly, we must warn them of the revulsion of feeling which is bound to take place. I will only refer very briefly to other matters which have cost us some public support. As regards Disestablishment, there is a very strong case for it in Wales, and in Scotland, in fact it is hard to say which country has the chief claim. The " pre- dominent partner "nevertheless is inclined to regard the question in each case from the English standpoint. But in England, Establishment is on a totally different foot- ing. Without a very large majority in favour of it,and a very strong feeling prevalent throughout the country against the existing order of things, Disestablishrnent is out of the question. On the other hand, where those conditions are fulfilled, it is only a question of time. Is England, we have neither condition. In Scotland and Wales, you have them both ; and many other circum- stances are combined to make a claim that it is illiberal and unjust to indefinitely resist and postpone, forcing on the country an Establishment which it neither respects nor requires. It seems to me that those who have at heart the maintenance of the English Establishment, will, in the end, only weaken their case by confounding it with the Church in Wales.

As to the liquor question, if there was a ballot to- morrow on the proposal to reduce the number of licensed premise(' in Warrington by one-fourtb, with fair notice and compensation, it may be to working publicans I be- lieve, the concensus of opinion would be in favour of it• Unfortunately a good deal of prejudice has been need- lessly aroused. They say no party can touch the liquor question without burning its fingers. If so, surely it was the more necessary that our leaders should be on their guard. It certainly seems a very serious error in tactics that we should have had offered to us the ex- tremes of total closing or remaining as we are. That proposal has been amended in the present Bill, but we suffer through the odium incurred, and I for one am bound to say, naturally incurred, by the original pro- posal, a proposal bound to be inoperative in the very districts where reform is most urgent. If it is made clear by the Temperance Party that their object is to re- duce the public-houses to a number which affords every- one reasonable convenience without thrusting, as it were, drink under the nose of work people gratuitoudY. in a word, and without going needlessly into detail, if they make reform and not abolition their object, being content to keep abreast of the times and educate opinion, then I think they are pretty certain to succeed. Sacri- fice in such a cause,any party should be willing to make. But we are not called upon to run our heads against a stone wall : and we must remember that the best of causes may be seriously damaged by bad generalship. Local Option is but e means to an end, but it appears to be the best means at hand. If the public-house is the poor man's wine cellar, then, as Mr. Burt said the other day, why not give him the key. I do not think we should wind up th;e brief list of the leading facts affecting our position as a party without mentioning one of the most important—the threatened issue with the Rouse of Lords. In the long run it will be to the advantage of the country and the party that this quc-stinn should be brought forward. In the mean- time Lord Rosebery suffers by it havieg fallen flat. It is too big an issue to be tacked on to other large ques- tions already to the fore. The country has more than enough on its mind already, and must have time to think this new question over, and to consider as alter- nativee,whether to reform the constitution of the Lords, or limit their Dowers, or whether to do both. It cer- tainly is no easy problem to solye,nor will the constituen- cies rush headlong into such a momentous reform. Most of us are, I think, files Lord ,Rosebery, Second Chamber men, but if our Second Chamber is to be not merely ornamental, but remain a real power, it will have to be reformed, and reformed very thoroughly too. Turning to another great item on our prngramm which may still cost us some support, clouded as the political horizon may be at the moment, and remote a local self-government for Ireland may therefore appear, this great measure is certain to he carried. It is only a question of time. The English people like the rest of the United Kingdom are sure to come to see that Ireland is as much entitled to thorough-going self-government as London is, and, ntvtatis mutandis, a solution of the question will probably be effected ou those lines in the end. There is no getting over the fact clear to demon- stration that a large measure of responsibility for the conduct of their own local governmsmt. will !vs not only beneficial to Ireland, but will add to the efficiency and capacity of the Imperial Parliament. Great, they sec., are the Uses of adversity. We may regret exceedingly the interruption to their work sue- tamed by the present Cabinet, composed of men wise are entitled to, and who have thoroughly earned our confi- dence and support. But should it be their fate to dwell for a time in the cool shade of opposition, they may seize the opportunity to develop to a still higher degree of perfection, the large measures of reform they have in hand. How long this period is likely to liter, assuming that the other side have a victory at the polls, aAd how, in that case the rwo wings of the Unionist or Conserva- tive Party will get on togrther, are interesting, questions to which time alone will afford an answer. If liberal- minded men in the Unionist Party are able to graft their ideas on the C mservatiye stock, then the alliance may have a long spell of authority over it. Be- cause, say what strong partisans will,moderate Liberal- ism commends the largest amount of support in the cnuntry, and its influence is increasing.

Whether You look in this country a; the Conservative re-aetion, or in Germany at the Lb^ral re-actinn,which broadly speaking, has set it, you see in each Ca-E1 that the people are realising for themselves in the most prac- tical fashion, Dr. Johnson's maxim that moderation is the floe.zt word in the English language. The danger is that the re-action of opinion may go too far. We h tve already advanced a long way in legislation which has for its watchwords "equality of opportunity, and the greatest good of the greatest nemher." But the work is unfinished, and while it remains so, the great fabric of our individualist Society also remains less healthy and IPsa absolutely secure than it ought to he. Di.) party need desire a greater or more inspiring object than the completion of that work,and I submit that events teach us we shall best achiev, it by treading the paths ot sound Lih.rali-m, refusing to turn aside in pursuit of the chimeras of Socialists and faddists—and achieva it too with most safetv and advantage to the individual and therefore to the nation.—Yours, &c., Warrington, June 25th, 1895.
A. H. bROSFIELD.

div.head: W ESTON.
div.p: W ESTON.

FUNERAL OF Me. IT. PEACOCK.—At Runcorn Cemetery on Friday afternoon the relNaias of Mr. H. Peacock, of Ford Bank-terrscr, Weston, were hid to r •st. Mr. Pea- cock was 24 years of age, and had been a member of the Weston Church Choir for several year, and as a tribute of respect the choir attended the funeral which was fully choral. The members of the choir marched from Weston in front of the hearse, each member carried his surplice on his arm, and each of the 22 boys carried a cross or wreath of fhwers in the other hand. This was the first choral funeral from the VillaZe of Weston and attracted considerable attention. The deceased • was very highly respected. On arriving at the cemetery chapel, the funeral was 'net by the Rev. W. FL Stables, curate-in-charge of Weston, who conducted the service. While the cefEn was tieing got ready the members of the choir passed into the chapel where they robed, and f,,vmingmund the east end and prayer desk, awaited the mourners. After the sentences had been said the choir chanted thP9o'.h Psalm, and after the lesson sang the hymn commencing, " How bright these glori•:,us spirits shine." Prayers were said in the chap 4 and the versicles, intoned by the choir. Then a procession was formed to the grave, the priest and choir marching first, singing the hymn " Brief life is here our portion." As the family arave was in the dissenters' portion of the cemetery the clerffym in first read the pr4yer of conse- cration,after which the rest of the service was prOC.Pded with. When it was ended the choir sang the closing hymn " Abide with Ma fast falls the eventide."

div.p: EARLESTO WN AN.D NEWTON.
DRI:TNKENNSEIS.
At the Town Hall, Newton on Tuesday morning, before Mr. C.B.F. Borron, a tramp named Frederick Le was charged with being drunk in Earlestown the previous evening, and was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

div.head: BOWLING MATCH.
div.p: BOWLING MATCH.

A match at bowls for .1:5 a aide was played on the green oi the Victoria Inn, IVargrave, on Saturday afternoon, between J. Hart of Golborne, and J. Abbott of Newton. The game was 101 up, and resulted in a win for Hart, the scores being, Hart 101, Abbott 86. LECTUER AT THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

A lecture was given in the Wesleyan Church, Earlestown, on Monday evening, by the Rev. John ityan,Nl.A.., on" Methodist Memories of America and Canada." The chair was occupied by Mr. J. bioun- cey, and there was a large congregation. The lec- ture was of an interesting character to Methodists, and dealt with the struggle of Methodism in America and Canada for 50 years back. A collection was made at the close on behalf of the Local Con- tingent Fund. TEIRPT FROM AN EARLRSTOWN SHOP.

Daniel Jones, of Mold, was charged at the War- rington Occasional Curt on Monday with having on the 11th or 12th May stolen 2ilb. beef, Ilb.ot ham and an ounce of tobazico. the property of Wil- liam Measures, of Legh-street,Earlestowu. He was further charged with having stolen a shirt, the pro- perty of James Jones, a lodger.—The prisoner, who nad been lodging at the house of Mr. Measures, ad- mitted the theft of all the articles named except the ham,and after several witnesses had been called he was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial.

div.head: ALLEGED THEFT OF TIMBER.
div.p: ALLEGED THEFT OF TIMBER.

At Newton Police Court on Saturday before C,)louel3d, William Bennett was charged with stealing four wood rafters from a brick yard off Houghton-street,Earlestown, sometime between the 17th and 20th hist, tne property of the executors George Poole, and valued at 103.—Edward Poole, executor, said that about 6 a in. on the 17th be saw a man named Tnomas Silver place some rafters and other boards besides the kiln in the brick yard' On the 20th he missed four,valued at 108. Later on he saw some of the timber in prisoner's house. Infor- mation.was given to the police and P.C.Green appre- hended the prisoner who admitted that the timber came from the brick yard.—Prisoner was remanded to the Petty Sessions held to day. Bail was al- lowed.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARY.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARY.

The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Templara was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening. Bro. W. Wilson presided, and there was a good attend- ance of members, including visiting brothers from the" Welcome " lodge Nelson. One candidate was initiated and arrangements were made for holding an open meeting next Monday evening. Several items of business affecting the interval working of the order were transacted The programme of the evening was" readings from the Temperance Com- panion," for which Bro. J. Hatton was responsibie. After a few remarks from him, a selection of ap- propriate readings were given by Bros. J. A nderton, E. Newman, G. Clarke, W. 11, Date, W. Wainwright and G. E. Warburton, Sisters S. Stringer, and R. Cordingley. Thanks were accorded to Bro. Hatton for his interesting programme.

div.head: WAIIGRAVB Citußcir CHOIR.
div.p: WAIIGRAVB Citußcir CHOIR.

The annual pic-nic in connection with the above took place on Saturday to Blackpool. The party, including the Rev. J. and Mrs. Carson, numbered 30, and left Newton Bridge by the 6.20 a.m. train, a comfortable saloon being provided for their con- venience. Through some delay on the line the train did not reach Blackpool until 10 o'clock, and a late breakfast was partaken of at the Station Hotel. The' remainder of the morning was spent on the North Pier, at the Eiffel Tower, and in a drive to the Cherry Tree gardens. Dinner was pro- vided at 1.45 at the same hotel, and being excel- lently served was heartily enjoyed. After dinner the party drove in a couple of waggonettes to Lytham, and on returning sat down to tea at the Station Hotel. The return journey for home was made by the 7.10 p.m. train, and reached Earles- stown about 930. The day was beautifully fine, and the outing V7a9 thoroughly enjoyed. ALLRORD_NEGLECT OF CHILDRRN r NRWTOX.

At the Town Hall, Newton, on Wednesday, betore Colonel Wood, William Henry Andrews and Mary Andrews, of 120, Mercer-st., Newton, were charged with wilfully and unlawfully illtreating and neg- lecting their children Edith, aged 11, William 9, Charles Edward 6, Lilly 5, Rosa 1 year and 10 months, on the 25th June and other dates during the last six months.—lnspector SlcAteer of the N.S.P.C.. Warrington, prosecuted, and his evidence went to show that the prisoners were drunken, and the house was in a filthy state and devoid of food arid furniture. The youngest child Rosa, weighed about 1311)4., and should have weighed about 251b5., and all the children were moreor less in a neglected and filthy condition and covered with vermin. The children were sent out begging and the motner was apprehenaed on Sunday night the worse for drink. Tne prisoners were remanded until Saturday. 1.0.0. T. (EBENEZER, LODGE)._

The usual weekly sesaion of the Earlestown libenezer Lodge No. 752, was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall on Tuesday. Session Was opened at 8 o'dock and was presided over by Bro. W. J. Taylor, there being a fair attendance of members and friends. Bro. Morris Jones, D. See, of Liverpool, was also present. The roll of officers was called and responded to. A communication was also read from the Temperance Mission Lodge, Warrington, accept- ing the invitation unanimously to visit the Hades- to wn Ehenezir LAige during the quarter, and they also tendered their fraternal greetings which were heartily received and the umal greetings exchanged. Programme of the evening, Bro. J. Taylor being responsible he invited a District Lodge officer, Bro. Morris Jones, D. Sec. of Liverpool, who gave a very instructive and stirring speech which was heartily appreciated, and an address was also given by Bro. Prance, of Leigh, which was also interesting. Votes of thanks were tendered to the speakers for their excellent addresses. Lodge was afterwards closed in due form at, 9.30. EARLIRSTOWN DAY SCHOOL'S TRIPS.

The annual trip given by Mr. T. moirieux., to the children attending the various day schools in Earles- town and Newton, for those who have not been absent on a single occasion during the year took place on Thursday to New Brighton. The morning opened very inauspiciously, a violent thunderstorm raging during the time the children were being put into the train, the heavy downpour of rain throwing all the arrangements into confusion. Happily however the 800 children and 80 teachers and managers were got away without mishap, and on arrival at Liverpo3l the elements were more favourable. Henceforward the day was beautifully fine, the children marching across the city to the binding stage in good order. The embarkation was quickly proceeded with, and on arrival at New Brighton, the youngsters dispersed over the and, and the tide being favourable they enjoyed them- selves waling in the water. Dinner and tea was partaken of in the Palace, and the homeward knit.- ney was commenced at 5.50, Earlestown being reached about 8 o'clock.

• TILE EXAMINER, !SATURDAY, JUNE 29 1895 TEMPERA.NC it' DEMONSTRA- TION AT RUNCORN. IN TE RESTING SPEECITES. At Runcorn on Tuesday evening a united temperance demonstration was held in support of local veto. An open-air demonstration was held in Devonshire Square about seven o'clock and, was largely attended. The speakers included the Rev. J. Safford, Mr. Thomas Hardy of Stoke-on-Trent, and others. A procession was afterwards formed and headed by the Weston Temper- ance Band, the processionists weiked to the Public Hall where a large and enthusiastic meeting was held. The chair was ocnupied by the Rev. T. Brackenbury, and he was supported on the platform by the Rev. Canon Hicks, M.A., of Manchester, Rev. J. C. Makin, of Liverpool, Mr. T. Wady, of Stoke-on-Trent, Revs. J. Hanby, of Fleetwood, J. H. Tite, and J. Stafford; Messrs. James Handley, J.P., Thomas Handley, J.P., William Handley, John Simpson, R. H. Posnett, G. Marshall, B. Kniyeton, D. Bisbrewn, T. Reynolds, J. Kirkham, and others. Letters of apology tor non-attecdance were read from the Rev. James Braman and Mr. T. Simister, and the Rev. John Simpson telegraphed "Sorry cannot come ; God's blessing attend your effort." After the singing of "On ward Christian Soidiers " and devotional exercises by the Rev. J. Hanby. Tho Chairman said he took the chair that evening at the request of a committee that had made the arrange- ments for that meeting. He did not feel at liberty to decline because he thought it was his duty to do what- ever he could to help any movement that was calculated to make England a sober nation. He was persuaded that the task of chairman would not be difficult or onerous. If anyone asked why there should be a meeting in favour of the Local Veto Bill in Runcorn the simple answer was, because there were people in R .ncorn who under- stood their duty asid meant to do it. It was quite true that the town of Runcorn was little compared with the ten great towns of their country, but after all Runcorn was a centre of considerable influence. It had about twice ten thousand inhabitants, some good, some bad, and some indifferent. The town had a considerable number of magistrates and councillors and constables to keep the town in order and it had a goodly number of churches and ministers, Senday school teachers and ether Christian workers who were trying to make the town a little more like paradise. Bait besides these it had a considerable number of public-kouses, and pub- licans, and strong drink disciples. There was one thing he observed about the public-houses and that was that they were too easy of access and they were too near to the door of the poet. householder. (Hear, hear.) As to the publicans he had not the least animosity against any- one of them. He supposed they were men all anxious to do business; eager to obtain profit, and the clietomers had the one good quality of paying ready money. Every house was a centre of temptation. People could easily get in but they found it difficult to get out. Times had been bad in Runcorn but there were better days in store when the Local Veto Bill became the law of the land. When the people said we can do without these public- houeea and their traffic, thea there would be a great revival of trade, and a great increase of happiness in a multitude of homes. (Applause.) They were there that night to show by their voice and vote that they were on the side of temperance, righteousness, and etrutli. 'they were there to send a message to statesmen to tell theta that they meant business ; to let them know that if they didn't give to the people the power to con- trol the drink traffic, they would know the reason why. (Applause.) He commended them to adopt the motto "We will have the Local Veto or know the reason why." (Applause.) The Rev, J. C. Watkin moved the followine resolution: —" That this meeting tenders its warmest thanks to Her Majesty's late Government for the introduction in Parliament of the Intoxicating Liquor Traffic (Local Control) Bill ; a measure which if passed into law,would very greatly help in the promotion of the social, moral, economic and political well-being of the people of this country ; and this meeting pledges itself to endeavour to secure the speedy enactment of this very valuable mea- sure." (Applause.) He said they wore-aware that the Government which introduced the Local Veto Bill had met with an unfortunate collision, and thus they !were in a state of disorder and " we don't know where we are." (Laughter.) There was one thing upon which Ithey could be clear and certain. They knew where the cause was. Parties might Come and parties might go ; Governments might arise and Governments might fall, hut the great cause which embodied the aspirations of a free and enlightened public lived on in spite of changes in the fortunes of parties and governments. (Applause.) He was delighted to say a word in support of the measure introduced into the House of Commons by the late Government. He wanted to assuee them that dense ignorance prevailed as to the nature of the provisions of the Bill. He found In his own congregation at Liverpool the densest possible ignorance as to the nature of the Bill. It was believed to no one for making everyone teetotal. Some Bei lit was intended to rob the poor man of his beer. They might take away his beef steak or almost anything but they must not touch his beer. (Laughter.) Then again some supposed it was going to make the brewers all paupers. It was his wish that when the Bill became law it would make. such tt change that the brewers would have to sing or say, since the passing of this heal option law we have got no work to do. (Laughter.) The Bill proposed in the first place to give to the electors of Runcorn the pewr to control this traffic in the town. It could not work in the absence of public opinion. If a tenth of the electors in any ward were desirous of put- ting the Bill in action they could request the authorities to have a vote on the question as to whether public. houses, with the exception of hotels, restaurants, and refreshment rooms, should remain open or net. If it was decided by a two-thirds majority that they should be closed, then all in the ward would be closed. If they were not ripe for total prohibition they might be, for an immediate 25 per cent, reduc- tion, and a majority would be sufficient for that. A majority would also be sufficient for Sunday closing, and he believed that in hundreds and thousands of wards and villages the people would only be deliehted to wipe out the stain of Sunday debauchery (Applause.) If people said they could not do without public-heuees then a bare majority bring them back again and they would be surrounded with them again. It was said that the teetotaler would coerce the moder- ate drinker. But the teetotaler was only one in nine,and he would have to persuade five moderate drinkers to vote with him before the bill could have any effect. It was impossible f-ar the teetotaler to coerce the moderate drinker. He appealed to his audience to help them in this great fight. He thought this great nation would arise to the demand that the bill made upon his moral sense and moral force, and that it would shake itself free from this infamous and horrible trade and reach forward I into newer and higher flights of happiness. (Applause.) The Rev. Canon Hicks in seconding the resolutiotnsaid they met that night under very strange And tryin, cir- cumstances for the Local Veto Bill was practically dead, because the Government that brought it forward had resigned. But still their cause and their crusade lived on. When they were making the concluding sentences to last year's report of the United Kingdom Alliance.and he was present as a representative of that Alliance, their . hearts were glad to think that a great Government had undertaken their cause. Their cause was bound up with the hepoinees and with the religious conviction of the country and therefore it was sure to prevail. They did not feel one wit differently on the question now that the Government had resigned. Their meetings would go on as before. He was glad to second the resolution because it expressed gratitude to the late Government for hav- ing espoused their cause. (Applause). He wished to speak a few words on the general aspects of the question. What were their fundamental principles as alliance men ? Firstly, that it was impossible for the common sale of drink to be carried on under whatever restrictions and safeguards se as not to he a nuisance and source of mis- chief in the neiehtemirtined whore it was carried on. Many differed from them in that respect, the Bishop of Chester, for instanee, who thought they could eliminate the common dangers mei provide snob safeguards as to make the traffic almost harmless. He did not think it would ever be simile:l4lllly tried. Their second prin- ciple was that the inhabitants of each locality should, if they pleased, expel the noxious traffic, and have the power to do so. It had been laid down in the Bill which had been expounded. Then they went in for the direct popular veto. They did not want it to be in the hands of Boards, Town Cmincils,er other municipal or elective bodies. They would not place between the will of the people And the eXeCtitiMl of their desire any sort of board whatever. 'These were their principles, and for them they meant to fight. (Applause.) Mr. Thomas Hardy in supporting the resolution said lhat meeting was the work of the ladies of Runcorn,and ha was glad they had been so far successful. He did not know a question on which there had been mere misreovsntation. Under pre:ent coorlitions he did not wonder why we had so many drunken people, he wondered why they had so teeny sober. There were paople who lived and got rich ty breaking the law and yet were never, brought to justice. He contended that publicans who made men drunk should be brought before the magistrates. (Ap- plause). The Chairman moved the adoption of the following BpPrittiatiionna'n—d'lrerloantdheinliPonaroluiarambeinet tass"eCerlemdoLiseolfiuGusrblet petition of the United Temperance Soc;eties of Runcorn aheweth that your petitioners recognizing that the greater part of tho misery, pauperism and crime of this country is inivetably consequent on the publichouse System, have heard with satisfaction of the introduction into the House or Commons by her Majesty's late Government of the Liquor Traffic (Local Control) Bills giving the inhabitants of districts power to veto the issue of licensed houses, and your petitioners pray your honourable house to press the above namediflill through all its steps with all possible speed."—The petition was approved of unanimously. A vote of thongs was accorded the speakers on the motion of the Rev.J.Stafford, seconded by the Rey 0.11. Tite.—Mr, William Handley proposed- a vote of thanks to the tnembers of the Weston brass band for their assistance.—Mr. Riabrown seconded the proposition and it was carried.—The Chairman was also thanked for his serviees on the motion of Mr. James Handley. J.Pe seconded by Mr. J. Kirkham. The ineetin then ter- ninated.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.

THE ACCIDENT AT LATCHFORD LOCK. On April 20th we inserted a report in the "Examiner" having reference to the accident to the Latchford Lock on the Manchester Ship Canal in which it was stated that Captain Smith of the "Harold " was under the in- fluence of drink at the time of the occurrence. The report in question,containing as it did serious reflections on the conduct of the captain of the" Harold," we have since been satisfied was absolutely unfounded, and we are anxious to do our utmost to remove any impressions calculated to injure Captain Smith which the report may have made. We unhesitatingly withdraw the state- ments complained ot, and sincerely apologise to Captain Smith tor having published them. IMPORTATION OF BUTTER. The City of Cork Steam Packet Company's fine new steamer %Primate was berthed at the Pomona Docks on Monday morning with a cargo of about 300 tons of butter, from Cork, consigned to Messrs. J. and J. Lons- dale, of this city. The whole consignment is being carted direct from the docks to the Cold Storage at Water-street which is thus used for the first time by direct shipments to the Manchester docks. Further shipments direct to Manchester are likely to follow. The Kenmare is the longest steamer that has yet been to the Pomona Docks, her length over all being 275 feet, whilst her gross ton- nage is 1,346 tons.

At the (dose of the attractive service held in the Arpley Roots, on Sunday,after the Benediction had been pronounced, Mr. Wildman said be had a very pleasant duty to perform, and that was to present to Miss Green a testimonial to show the affection and respect in which she is held by her railway friends in whom she is so deeply interested. They wished to show her how much her efforts on their behalf were appreciated, and as an expression of their esteem and love they asked her to accept the gift they were offering. Miss M. E. Dindiey then brought a desk to the table, which she pre- sented with a letter in which much appreciation of Miss Green's work was expressed. Miss Green cordially thanked the kind friends who had ex- pressed such good wishes on her behalf, and who had given her such a aseful and handsome present. For a long time she had felt that the interest that she took in her railway friends was warmly re- sponded to by them,and this agreeable surprise was a proof of it. PRESENTATION TO A CHESHIRE LINES OFFICIAL.

On Fri,- lay evening a number of the staff of the Glazebrook Station of the Cheshire Lines Committee met in the gentlemen's waiting-room in order to make a presentation to Mr. Thomas Oakes, station- master, who is leaving shortly to take up the more important duties of goods agent at the M.S.& L.Ry. Co.'s new goods station at St. Helens. Mr. J. E. Tonge, pointsman, placed upon the table a splendid briar and amber pipe with mountings in solid silver, a pouch, and a supply of tobacco. Mr. George Ashton,signalman,iu a lew well chosen words,asked Mr. Oakes to accept them as a small token of the regard in which he lies been held by the staff dur- ing the liso years he has had charge of Glazebrook Station. In reply Mr. Oakes said the presentation was a great surprise to him,and he wished to thank one and all for the very kindly way in which they met him in this particular instance,and also for the very able mariner in which they had at all times assisted him in dealing with the traffic, &c., ex- changed at that station. He trusted that whoever his successor might be they would extend to him the same assistance, and that he in return would fake an equal interest in the welfare of the staff, thus ensuring a continuance of the pleasure and harmony in discharging their respective duties that had existed up to the present date. The shocking burning accident at Longford-st., which we reported in our last issue, in Which Mrs. Caldwell, of L 0 Longford-street,was severely burnt by her clothes catching fire, resulted in her death on Saturday morning at the Warrington Infirmary. The inquest was held by Mr. Bnghoustl at tile Police Station on Monday, Mr. A. Browne being present on behalf of the relatives.—Ann Boscow. sister of the deceased, said that Mrs. Caldwell was 65 years of Age. She saw her on Friday afternoon at the Infirmary, but she made no statement as to how the accident had taken place.—Nurse Hill said that the deceased died at 10.30 a.m. on Saturday. She nevet made any statement to her.--Elizabeth Bement', servant to deceased, said that she and her mistress were engaged tarring a shed in the back yard. 'I here was a tire between some bricks to melt the tar which was in a pot. The tar pot had been pulled off the fire and placed on a bench. Mrs. Caldwell went into the house to put some coals on the fire, and when she came out again,she cried out that she was on fire. Witness Who was on a wall , was:going to get down to try and put out the flames when the deceased ran screaming Into the next door but one. The flames were afterwards put out by some neighbours.—Alban Tickle said that he heard the screams, and got a coat and some rugs and succeeded in extinguishing the flames but burnt his hands severely in the act. He went for , doctor,hut when he returned he found that Mrs. Caldwell had been taken to the Infirmary.—Mr. A. Browne said that be understood that Mr. H. Taylor, P.C.M., had also come to the deceased woman's assistance. The jury returned a verdict of " Acci- dental Death." Mr. Browne wished to thank on behalf of the family, Mr. Taylor, Mr. Tickle, and all others who assisted in extinguishing the flames, and also the police who had brought their ambul- ance to take her to the Infirmary. WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday. Mr. W. Houghton presided, and there were also present Mrs. Clay, the Revs. CI. F. Roberts, T. R. Matthews, Messrs. S. Davies G. Pilling, A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, J. Clarke, W. Shaw, Lang, W. Hickman, J. W. Knowles, J. Houghton, J. Bi!lenge, E. L. Bent ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (deputy clerk), C. H. Ward (master), El. M. Mines (superintendent). GIFTS. The Mamma reported that Mr. Broadbent had pre- sented a number of pictures which required framing be- fore they were placed in the wards.

HOUSE COMMITTEL This Committee recommended that the matron of the Workhouse be allowed 14 days leave of absence at con- venient times.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Clarke, seconded by Mr. A. J. Jolley. Mr. Clarke said that the only item worthy of mention was a rise in nurse's salary. It was an understanding that the nurses received an increase at the end of 12 months.

SCHOOLS COMMITTER. The 8.7.h001s Committee recommended that the usual treat be allowed the children on Walking day, and that the children's railway fare from Padgate to Warrington be paid; that the school mistress and the assistant school master be allowed 14 day's leave of absence ; and also that Mr. Taylor's bill for work at the schools be not paid. —Mr. Davies in proposing the adoption of the minutes said that with reference to Mr. Taylor's bill, the commit- tee were a little divided. The bill bad been sent to Mr. Taylor a short time ago for revision, the committee thinking that he had overcharged them. Mr. Taylor had sent his bill back again saying that the charges were such that he could make no reduction.—The Clerk: Is the charge in excess of what he he has previously charged P—Mr.Davies 41 believe not.—The Clerk : Then I say clearly you are out of court. The only thing is for you not to give him further employment. I would ad- vise you to pay the bill.—Mr. Knowles said that was his opinion, but the majority was in favour of going to the County Court. The clerk did not think there was any case for the County Court—Mr. Clarke said hisopinion was that committee should not sanction the payment of the bill, but leave it to the Board to decide.—Mr. Hickman and Mr. Cross considered the bill was excessive, but as there was no other course left open,thty agreed that it be paid this time. It was finally decided to pay the bill and satisfaction was expressed that in future as the Build- ing and Repairs Committee had been formed, the Board could have the advice of that committee in similar cases in future.

EXTENSION OF LHE BOROUGH: UNEXPECTED RESULT. Fhe CLERX read a notice received from the Local Government Board granting the application of the War- zington Corporation to extend the borough boundary. He said that he had written in reply, stating that in his opinion the centre of the Ship Canal would have been a more equitable boundary than the northern bank. In his evidence at the inquiry he had expressed the same opinion, but considering the opposition which would have been encountered had that been applied for, it was considered advisable that the boundary should be the northern bank. Little Sankey would be included in St. Austin's ward, which would extend from Bridge-at. to Sankey Bridges. This was out of proportion to the other wards of the borough. It might be that the Cot, porstion intended to alter the bonnaaries of the wards of the town in some future time. Mr. Hickman would keep his seat as member of St. Austin's, but it was unfortunate that they would lose the services of Mr. Thompson. He had received a letter from Mr. Thompson (who was unable to attend the meeting) which stated stated that, if correct informed, he would lose his seat on the Board. Be was told loy the Clerk that he should lose his seat on the District Council, but retain tus seat on the Board of Guardians. He distinctly remembered the question being asked at the past meeting when the moticn to entend the Borough was passed, and they were assured that Little Sankey would retain its inem- her on the Board. The Clerk continuing said that he was surprised to find by the provisional order that Little Sankey would he merged into St. Austin's Ward. The portions of the Cheshire parishes added would also be added to the Latchford ward. The extension of the borough was purely a matter for the Corporation. He was sure that they would all be sorry to lose the services of Mr. Thompson. (Hear hear)—Mr. A. Jolley asked what was the boundary of the ward he represented (Latchford)—The clerk ; you will represent as far as the Ship Canal. I wanted them to put you in the middle, but they would not let me. (Loud laughter.)—Mr. Hick- man expressed his regret at losing the serviccs of Mr. Thompson.—The Clerk said that he had another letter from Mr. Thompson resigning his seat on the Infirmary Committee.—This resignation was accepted on the motion of Mr. Davies seconded by Mr. J. Houghton.— Mr. A. Jolley proposed, and Mr. Lang secondedo hat Mr. Rickman be elected to the vacant position.—Mr. Knowles proposed Mr. Halton, but as there as no seconder, Mr. Hickman was elected.

He wished to corroborate Mr. Berry when he sal t that his receipts had been Nit ing off.—The Clerk Raid that the imperial tax was paid by arrangement between the landlord and his tenant, who agreed to pay the rates. The county rates were now very much larger than formerly, and if the assess- ment of the houses by the Committee were not the same as the county assessment,it would practically amount to the fact that the other ratepayers would have to pay part of the rates for the house.—Mr. Bent however still expressed his opinion that the public houses were ast,essed too high.

div.head: PREPARATIONS FOR THE FIGHT.
div.p: PREPARATIONS FOR THE FIGHT.

In view of the corning General Election, the General Purposes Committee of the National Liberal Federation has met during the week in London, and the secretary of the Federation was instructed to issue a circular letter to the various Liberal and Radical associations throughout the country advising them as to the courso to adopt when the dissolution is announced. Equal activity was observable at the Conservative headquar- quarters. Advices from all parts of the country snow that preparations are being pushed forward with ex- traordinary' vigour. It is expected that all the leading members of the Liberal party,including Sir Wilti,m ar - court, will take a very active part in the campaign. There are 670 seats in the House of Commons,distributed as follows :—England, 465 ; Wales, 30 ; Scotland, 72 ; and Ireland, 103. In Ireland it is not anticipated thai. more than forty or filty of the 103 seats will be contested by the Unionists ; but in Great Britain, out of 567 seats they will have candidates, it is said, in all but about 20 instances.

The Press Association states that Mr. John Redmond has announced that it is a settled and deliberate inten- tion of the Panteßites to contest every constituency in Ireland at the approaching election. The Irish National League of Great Britaint the body which attends to the organisation of Irish Nationalist voters in this country, has sent an urgent circular to every branch of the association. Great importance is attached to constitaencies. over 100 in number, where the Irish vote is alleged to hold the balance of power. The Nationalists have, it is said, been cheered for the approaching contest by a piece el most acceptable good fortune in the shape of an offer from four Irish sym- pathisers to guarantee each the sum of £5,000 (£20,000 in all) for the benefit of the election fund.

The' Nationil Union of Elementary Teachers have made several attempts to obtain direct representation in the House of Commons. In the forthcoming contest Mr. Yoxall, the general secretary of the Union, will stand as a Liberal in a Nottingham division, and Mr. Ernest Gray, 11.1. A., will contest North-West [lam against Mr. Archibald Grove. The officials of the Union regard the prospects of both candidates as hopeful. Mr. James Hayeman is the candidate for Mile-end. . . .

The following ministerial appointments have been an- nounced. Lord Salisbury in addition to the Premiership, will take the Secretaryship for Foreign Affairs. Mr. Balfour is to be First Lord of the Treasury, Mr. Cham- berlain Secretary for the Colonies, the Duke of Devon- shire Lord President of the Council, Sir M. Flicks-Beach Chanceller of the Exchequer, Mr. Goschen First Lord of the Admiralty, and Mr. Chaplin President of the Local Government Board.

Addressing a meeting at Hammerswith on Thursday night, Mr. Tom Mann, general secretary of the Indepen- dent Lahrty party,referred to the attitude that p•irty would take up towards Liberals and Conservatives at the general election. He said that whilst the Indepen- dent Labour party were fully alive to the fact that they were a relatively young and small organisation there were nevertheless, apart from those constituencies where they themselves were running candidates, thirty others where for a certainty they could control at least 250 votes in each. There were also 50 other constitu- encies where they could control 150 votes, so that although the party was small they could really decide the fate of quite 60 to 70 constituencies. The party's probable attitude would be abstention where there was not a 8 )cialist candidate, but the conference to be held on the 4th July would consider any other easeq, irrespective of the party they belonged to—(hem, hear), —with a view of seeing whether some could be exempt from the hostility of the Independent Labour party.

A BOOK FOR MARRIED WOMEN. The information contained in this book ought to be known by every married woman, and it will not harm the unmarried to read. The book is cmveniently divided into 12 chapters. The first chapter treats of the changes at puberty, or when a girl becomes a woman. The second chapter treats of marriage from a doctor's standpoint ; points out the best age or marriage, and who should have children and who not, and furnishes useful information that one can ordinarily get only from an intelligent doctor. The third chapter treats of the marriage of blood relations; and condemns such marriages as a rule. Chapter four treats of the signs of pregnancy. The fifth chapter tells how a woman should live during the pregnant state. The sixth chapter treats of mishaps and how to avoid them. The seventh chapter treats of maternal impressions and shows that birthmarks are not due to longings i. n the part of the mother, b4t rather to her poor health. The eighth chapter teaches how to have easy confinements. Certain people believe that women should bring forth in pain and trouble, but the hygienic, ph% sician says that confinements can be made comparatively ea..y i certain rules are obeyed ; these rules are given. The ninth chapter treats of the proper management of confin.ment until the baby is born. The tenth chapter tells how to treat the mother till she is up and about again. The eleventh chapter treats or sterility ; gives the main eauses of it, bow these may be overcome and children result The last chapter treats of the "change," a most important article tor at women over forty. The book is full of useful information, and no book is written which goes so thoroughly into matters relating to married women. Some may think too much is told ; such can scarcely be the case. for knowledge is power and the means of attaining happiness. The book cal be had from Or, T. R.
